articles.title: She once worked in fields for ₹200 and saved ₹100 a day; today Maharashtra's Sunita Nehare manages her family's 12-acre farm after transforming its cotton harvest
articles.summary: At 4 am, Sunita Nehare would begin her household chores. By 6 am, she would be working as a farm labourer, earning ₹200 for two hours of work.
articles.body: At 4 am, Sunita Nehare would begin her household chores. By 6 am, she would be working as a farm labourer, earning ₹200 for two hours of work. After that, she would head to her family’s own fields and work until 1 pm. Every day, she put ₹100 from her wages into a post office savings account. Today, the 12 acres of family land that she once had little say in managing have become her responsibility. Sunita, who lives in Pachod village in Maharashtra’s Wardha district, has improved cotton production, brought unused plots under cultivation and diversified the farm with pulses, millets and other crops.As reported by Down To Earth, Sunita’s cotton yield has risen from around 1-1.5 quintals per acre to 7.14 quintals per acre. Intercropping cotton with red gram gives her an additional 2.75 quintals of the pulse. Her story is not just about increasing farm output. It is also about what changed when she gained the authority to decide how the family’s land would be cultivated.From working as a labourer to managing her family's landWhen Sunita married into the family, only about 3.5 acres of its 12 acres were being cultivated. Her ageing father-in-law managed the farm, while her husband had grown frustrated by repeated poor harvests from the rain-fed fields and had turned to alcohol. The sloping land lost rainwater quickly, and wild boars, nilgai and rabbits damaged crops. Farming offered little certainty. According to Agro News Today, when Sunita’s daughter was four, an argument with her husband made her consider leaving the house. Her father-in-law intervened and offered her responsibility for cultivating the land so she could support the family. She decided to stay and take charge of farming.According to Agro News Today, she began with nine rows of cotton in 2018. The first harvest yielded five quintals. She experimented with sowing patterns, manure and irrigation, and production rose to eight quintals the following year. Over time, the harvest from those 3.5 acres increased to 25 quintals. Water remained a major problem. Sunita collected monsoon rainwater in a pit near the farm and used an engine to pump it onto the cotton crop. In 2024, she dug a well with support from a state government scheme. She now spends around ₹12,000 each season on diesel to run the irrigation engine.How she changed the way the farm is cultivatedSunita received support through the Climate Change Adaptation Project, implemented by the Wardha-based nonprofit Dharamitra with support from the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) She adopted several practices to conserve soil moisture, improve fertility and reduce the risks associated with relying on a single crop. Sunita prepares bio-inputs such as Jeevamrit, Dashaparni Ark and Beej Amrit, and uses neem oil for crop protection. According to Down To Earth, she applies six tractor-trolley loads of cow dung manure annually across alternate plots and returns red gram and soybean residues to the soil. She says she no longer uses urea. She has also brought previously uncultivated land back into production. After clearing shrubs, levelling plots and strengthening the field bunds with stones, she began growing jowar, bajra, green gram and sesame. Crop rotation allows her to avoid planting the same crop on a plot every year.Wild animals continue to threaten the harvest. She uses solar-powered fencing and reflective strips to deter wild boars and nilgai, while nets protect selected plots from rabbits. An exposure visit to Nashik gave her another idea: planting fruit trees along the farm bunds. She has planted mango, guava, cashew, jackfruit and lemon trees, which she hopes will provide another source of income as she grows older.Farm earnings reach ₹2.5 lakh, including savings on foodAccording to Down To Earth, Sunita’s earnings from cotton, red gram and other crops have exceeded ₹2 lakh over the past two to three years. Growing green gram, black gram and vegetables for household consumption saves the family an estimated ₹14,760 a year in purchases. Poultry sales contribute another ₹10,000. Together, these farm earnings and savings amount to approximately ₹2.5 lakh, excluding income from her other activities. Sunita has also diversified her livelihood beyond crop cultivation. She works as a 'Pashu Sakhi,' a village-level livestock resource person who assists with vaccinations, administers medicines and maintains records. The work earns her around ₹3,000 a month, which she uses for household expenses and life insurance premiums.Her family life has changed tooThe changes extend beyond the fields. According to Down To Earth, Sunita’s elder child studies in Class 12 at a military school, while her daughter is in Class 6 at the village school. The family has also built a house in Pachod. Her work as a Pashu Sakhi and volunteer often requires her to travel between villages, sometimes returning home at night after walking long distances. Seeing these difficulties, her father-in-law bought her a two-wheeler to make travel to farms, meetings and neighbouring villages easier.Sunita believes that saving and financial planning matter particularly for households with limited incomes. Her own habit of putting aside ₹100 from her daily wages began when she had little control over the family farm. But she is also realistic about farming. Rainfall has become less predictable, she says, and farmers have little control over market prices. Cultivation requires substantial labour, and she does not want her son to depend entirely on agriculture because she is unsure whether farm income alone can sustain a family.You use AI every day. articles.title: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder
articles.summary: France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday.
articles.body:
Thunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend's mayhem, illuminating the cracked windows and boarded-up doors of hundreds of businesses that were smashed as protests gave way to disorder.

France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, and the majority looted.

A police union boss told the BBC that the weekend had been an "apocalyptic" hell for his colleagues. 118 officers were injured, representing more than a tenth of the national figure.

So far, 101 arrests have been made in the port city, a quarter of them children.

But by Monday, it was police who were most conspicuous on the city's streets, not protesters. For eight hours, demonstrations and gatherings were banned in an effort to avoid a third consecutive day of disorder.

It seemed to work; the largest central gathering we witnessed was a posse of weather-beaten tourists trudging around the quayside.

Nonetheless, an overnight curfew for minors is expected to be announced for some parts of the city from Tuesday.

Marseille is one of France's most ethnically diverse cities – a place where generations of new arrivals have landed.

18-year-old student Maryame only arrived in the southern city a few weeks ago, albeit from the countryside not too far away.

"It was very scary because it's my first time in a big city, and also my first time demonstrating," she said.

Maryame said violence engulfed the student demonstration her friends had joined as looters began attacking shops.

She said the solidarity of the earlier march was "beautiful" and the subsequent disorder "terrifying", but went on to say that she was conflicted as to whether even more violence would make the government sit up and listen.

"It is a very complicated question if violence is legitimate," she began.

"But the thing is, France, our history is really based on revolution, and sometimes we really have to make a really big impact.

For the police, the extent to which order disintegrated was a shock, according to one organisation representing rank and file officers.

"It was a war," said Arnaud Blaise from the UN1TE police union. "An unheard-of level of violence. Unprecedented."

Looting was reported across the city centre, including along La Canebière - Marseille's equivalent of Paris's Champs-Élysées - Rue Paradis, and at the Centre Bourse shopping centre. Businesses were also hit further afield, such as in the Grand Littoral and Le Merlan shopping malls to the north.

Blaise said he was concerned that future protests could follow the same destructive pattern as Saturday, with young people from the deprived northern suburbs seizing the opportunity to steal amid chaos that, in his view, was stirred up by far-left agitators - referred to in France as the Black Bloc.

"The Black Blocs provoked, and the youngsters took advantage to start looting," Blaise said. "That created chaos, with police officers running right, running left, and in effect, we got overwhelmed."

I put it to Blaise that the police had been accused of heavy-handedness with peaceful students but sitting back as the most violent protesters pillaged local businesses.

"That is not the case at all," he replied, arguing that more police than students had been injured.

"Four thousand tear gas grenades were fired and then we ran out of ammunition. So at a certain point, you have no choice but to retreat."

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez - whose resignation in the wake of the riots was rejected by President Macron - travelled to Marseille on Monday evening.

He came to the City Hall, which was briefly occupied by protestors on Saturday, and met Marseille's Socialist Mayor Benoît Payan.

Payan said he wanted answers from the government as to how the chaos was allowed to happen.

"Order was lost, and an attempt was made to restore order. I believe that from start to finish, it was a fiasco," he said on Monday.

He said under-staffed and poorly deployed police needed to change their tactics.

"If there isn't a radical change of approach on this issue - if, by chance, the only target remains high school students - then we will see looting scenes again."

He continued: "I don't know what's left to loot in Marseille, but for the little that remains, it will be looted."

While the ban on public gatherings in Marseille and partial overnight curfews in other French cities have brought some temporary calm, more demonstrations are planned for the weekend.

At a smashed out tram stop, 79-year-old grandmother Chantal Bellanger said she had been "worried - but then, I've been worried for a long time".

"We can clearly see that France has lost its grip on many things. Public services, hospitals, education is in a horrible state, the peripheral neighbourhoods are dilapidated, they are abandoned."

She said she used to work in these deprived northern suburbs, where poverty and crime rates are very high, and feared a whole lost generation was criminalising itself through anger and despair.

"It tugs at your heartstrings," she said.

"To see children whose actions are going to place them completely outside of society. It's painful to watch."

Additional reporting by Paul Pradier and Pol Reygaerts

articles.title: Enem 2026: é melhor chutar ou deixar questões em branco? Entenda a TRI | G1
articles.standfirst: Teoria de Resposta ao Item avalia a coerência no desempenho. Candidato terá menos pontos se acertar as questões muito difíceis, mas errar as mais fáceis. Deixar de responder pode prejudicar ainda mais a nota.
articles.summary: Teoria de Resposta ao Item avalia a coerência no desempenho. Candidato terá menos pontos se acertar as questões muito difíceis, mas errar as mais fáceis.
articles.body:
Caderno de resposta, prova, exame, concurso, Enem — Foto: Eduardo Ribeiro Jr./g1

"Chutar" as respostas no Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) pode não ser uma boa estratégia para tentar garantir uma nota alta: há o risco de o desempenho final do candidato ser prejudicado. No entanto, deixar de responder uma questão é uma opção ainda pior.

Mas por quê? É que a nota final não é simplesmente a soma do número absoluto de acertos . O método de correção usado na prova, chamado de Teoria de Resposta ao Item (TRI), prioriza o desempenho que for coerente .

“A TRI não faz uma simples contagem de acertos. Ela observa o conjunto das respostas para estimar o nível de conhecimento que o estudante demonstrou. É esperado, por exemplo, que quem consegue resolver questões mais difíceis também acerte boa parte das mais fáceis”, explica Vanessa Santos, gerente de Projetos Educativos e Avaliação Educacional do Poliedro Educação.

Dois alunos que acertarem exatamente o mesmo número de perguntas podem tirar notas diferentes. O raciocínio por trás disso é que, se alguém acerta as questões mais difíceis, mas erra aquelas consideradas fáceis, provavelmente "chutou" as respostas. Por isso, terá uma nota inferior à de um estudante que acertou as fáceis, mas errou as mais complexas (veja ilustração abaixo) .

Dois participantes acertaram 5 respostas. Veja só como aquele que errou justamente as mais fáceis tirou uma nota menor do que o outro, que errou as difíceis. — Foto: Reprodução/Inep

A TRI apresenta as seguintes vantagens em relação ao método clássico de correção:

ao detectar os famosos "chutes", ela premia o aluno que, de fato, se preparou para a prova;

possibilita a comparação entre candidatos que tenham feito diferentes edições do exame;

torna mais improvável que dois concorrentes tirem exatamente a mesma nota.

✅ Qual estratégia usar para se dar bem na TRI?

Gastar energia, logo de cara, com aquela pergunta muito longa e complexa pode cansar o aluno e fazer com que ele erre, depois, uma questão considerada simples. No contexto de TRI, a nota será prejudicada.

Na 1ª leitura: resolver todas as questões que considerar fáceis.

Na 2ª leitura: responder às perguntas em que tiver ficado entre duas alternativas, consideradas médias.

Na 3ª leitura: fazer as questões mais longas ou sobre assuntos não tão comuns no Enem, consideradas difíceis.

👉🏽Fazer a prova nessa ordem pode ajudar a aumentar a nota em relação ao sistema TRI. Neste caso, se o aluno deixar para responder por último as questões que achar difíceis, e se precisar chutar, a nota não vai ser tão comprometida caso ele erre a resposta.

Apesar de priorizar um desempenho coerente, a TRI não anula a nota caso um aluno acerte as questões difíceis e erre as fáceis. Neste caso, o padrão de respostas vai identificar uma variação e vai atribuir uma nota menor a este acerto, do que atribuiria caso os itens mais fáceis também estivessem corretos.

“A TRI não é detetive de chute. Acertar uma questão nunca faz a nota cair. O que pode acontecer é aquele acerto ter uma contribuição menor no resultado quando analisado dentro do padrão de respostas daquele estudante”, afirma Vanessa.

📈 Por que a nota da prova não vai de 0 a 1.000?

No Enem 2025, a nota máxima na prova de Linguagens, por exemplo, foi 794,5 e a mínima, 309,2.

Ou seja: quem acertou todas não tirou 1.000, e quem errou 100% das perguntas não ficou com zero. Por quê?

Segundo o Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (Inep), que organiza e aplica o Enem, o que determina os "extremos" da nota é o grau de dificuldade das perguntas daquela edição .

"Quando a prova for composta por muitos itens fáceis, o máximo tenderá a ser mais baixo, e quando for formada por itens difíceis, o mínimo tenderá a ser mais alto", diz o órgão, em documento de orientação aos participantes.

🚨 Mas, atenção: deixar uma questão em branco nunca é a melhor opção . O ideal é se preparar para o exame, para que, mesmo sem saber responder tudo, o a candidato apresente um desempenho "coerente".

articles.title: Marco Nanini: retirada de intérprete de Libras de peça põe lei à prova | G1
articles.standfirst: Apresentação da peça 'Fim de Partida' no Teatro Simões Lopes Neto, em Porto Alegre, seguiu sem acessibilidade. Produtora alegou problema de iluminação e admitiu falha na organização do evento.
articles.summary: Apresentação da peça 'Fim de Partida' no Teatro Simões Lopes Neto seguiu sem acessibilidade. Produtora alegou problema de iluminação e admitiu falha na organização do evento
articles.body:
Uma apresentação da peça "Fim de Partida", estrelada por Marco Nanini , no Teatro Simões Lopes Neto, em Porto Alegre , causou polêmica no último domingo (18). O motivo foi que o ator pediu que os intérpretes de Língua Brasileira de Sinais (Libras) fossem retirados do palco .

Porém, considerando a Lei Brasileira de Inclusão (LBI), o intérprete de Libras não pode ser retirado durante uma apresentação, pois deve ser garantida a acessibilidade da pessoa com deficiência em igualdade de condições .

Segundo espectadores, o ator alegou que a iluminação sobre os intérpretes atrapalhava sua performance e pediu que eles saíssem. A sessão foi interrompida e, minutos depois, o espetáculo continuou sem acessibilidade , o que fez com que pessoas se retirassem — por necessitarem do intérprete ou em protesto pelo ocorrido. As cortinas se fecharam e o público vaiou Nanini .

A legislação garante que pessoas com deficiência tenham direito à cultura, ao esporte, ao turismo e ao lazer. A LBI assegura o acesso a programas de televisão, cinema, teatro e outras atividades em formato acessível.

Conforme o texto, é proibida a recusa de oferta de qualquer obra intelectual em formato acessível para pessoas com deficiência. Segundo o artigo 42, é vedada a recusa "sob qualquer argumento”.

A lei prevê, ainda, que as normas de acessibilidade devem ser asseguradas nos locais de eventos e nos serviços prestados pelas entidades organizadoras das atividades culturais.

A legislação, no entanto, não obriga que casas de espetáculos tenham intérpretes em libras. Nesse caso, a acessibilidade estava sendo ofertada previamente .

"A legislação não estabelece obrigatoriedade expressa de que todas as casas de teatro tenham um intérprete de libras. Agora, estava sendo ofertado, e interromper esse recurso no meio da apresentação me parece um problema jurídico importante, às vezes sem a intenção, mas pode caracterizar uma certa forma de discriminação da pessoa com deficiência", analisa o mestre em Direito e professor da PUCRS, Plínio Melgaré.

Sem a oferta da interpretação em libras, o público foi diretamente afetado naquela apresentação. Na plateia, havia pessoas com deficiência auditiva que relataram frustração e constrangimento com o ocorrido.

"O ponto central de todo esse problema é a efetiva acessibilidade. Não está em causa apenas garantir que as pessoas com deficiência acessem fisicamente a sala de espetáculo, ao teatro, mas sim que eles possam participar. O que está em causa também é eliminar as barreiras comunicacionais que são enfrentadas pelas pessoas com deficiência", completa.

O g1 tenta contato com o ator Marco Nanini, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Em nota, a produtora Pequena Central de Produções Artísticas justifica que "foi identificado um problema de compatibilidade entre o posicionamento da intérprete de Libras e a iluminação do espetáculo" e admite que "falhou ao não verificar e garantir previamente as condições técnicas necessárias à realização da sessão com interpretação em Libras".

A Fundação Theatro São Pedro, responsável pelo espaço cultural, lamenta o ocorrido e afirma que "apesar das possibilidades avaliadas e dos esforços empreendidos, não foi possível encontrar uma solução que contemplasse todas as necessidades envolvidas naquele momento, e a peça voltou a ser apresentada sem a interpretação de Libras".

Essa foi a segunda apresentação do espetáculo na capital gaúcha. A primeira sessão ocorreu na noite de sábado (17), sem registro de intercorrências.

O texto clássico de Samuel Beckett é encenado por Marco Nanini, Guilherme Weber, Helena Ignez e Ary França.

Caso Marco Nanini: retirada de intérprete de Libras do palco de peça põe à prova a Lei Brasileira de Inclusão, em vigor há 11 anos — Foto: Roger Lerina/Arquivo pessoal

Uma das espectadoras da sessão, a gestora cultural e professora de teatro Izabel Cristina da Silveira, relatou que o problema com a iluminação foi levantado por Nanini já no início do espetáculo . Segundo ela, a apresentação foi interrompida depois que o ator afirmou que a sombra provocada pela luz sobre a intérprete estava prejudicando sua visão .

"Já no início do espetáculo, o ator Marco Nanini falou sobre a questão da sombra que a luz na intérprete estava projetando no palco e que isso estava incomodando a visão dele. E o espetáculo parou", conta Izabel.

Segundo a professora, os atores pediram que fossem fechadas as cortinas devido a um problema técnico . Em seguida, as duas intérpretes de Libras saíram do local. "Imediatamente saí também do teatro e algumas outras pessoas saíram, outras ficaram revoltadas, indignadas."

"Eu quase não acreditei no que estava vendo acontecer, quando Nanini parou a apresentação e falou daquela maneira. Estou ainda incrédula que a maioria das pessoas permaneceu lá assistindo o espetáculo como se nada tivesse acontecido", completa.

O ator surdo Lucas Bourscheid também estava na plateia e relatou momentos de frustração e constrangimento após a retirada dos intérpretes de Libras do palco.

Para o espectador, situações como essa têm um impacto que vai além de uma apresentação específica. Ele ressalta que a retirada de um recurso de acessibilidade durante um espetáculo pode provocar um sentimento de exclusão.

“Se pedir para cancelar o intérprete de Libras na frente da plateia, é muita tristeza. Pode destruir a vontade de assistir, pode causar impacto emocional”, afirma.

Bourscheid defende que produções culturais levem a acessibilidade em consideração desde a concepção dos espetáculos e que artistas e equipes estejam preparados para receber diferentes públicos.

"A arte é para todos e a comunidade surda tem o direito de participar, compreender e vivenciar o espetáculo em sua própria língua, a Libras", comenta o espectador.

A Pequena Central de Produções Artísticas, produtora do espetáculo Fim de Partida, vem a público esclarecer o ocorrido na sessão deste domingo, 18 de outubro, no Teatro Simões Lopes Neto, em Porto Alegre, anunciada com audiodescrição e interpretação em Libras.

Durante a apresentação, foi identificado um problema de compatibilidade entre o posicionamento da intérprete de Libras e a iluminação do espetáculo. A sessão foi brevemente interrompida para que a produção e a equipe da Fundação Theatro São Pedro buscassem uma solução. Não foi possível resolver o problema naquele momento, e a apresentação foi retomada sem interpretação em Libras, comprometendo o acesso do público surdo ao espetáculo.

Reconhecemos que a produção falhou ao não verificar e garantir previamente as condições técnicas necessárias à realização da sessão com interpretação em Libras neste teatro. Assumimos inteira responsabilidade por essa falha e por suas consequências.

Pedimos sinceras desculpas, especialmente ao público surdo prejudicado, às intérpretes e às demais pessoas envolvidas.

A acessibilidade integra nosso compromisso com o público e precisa ser assegurada também no planejamento e na execução de cada apresentação."

"A Fundação Theatro São Pedro informa que, durante a apresentação do espetáculo Fim de Partida, realizada neste domingo (18), no Teatro Simões Lopes Neto, ocorreu uma intercorrência técnica envolvendo a iluminação destinada ao serviço de interpretação em Libras.

Diante da situação, a equipe da Fundação atuou diretamente na mediação entre os envolvidos, buscando alternativas técnicas que permitissem a continuidade do espetáculo e a manutenção das condições adequadas de acessibilidade. Apesar das possibilidades avaliadas e dos esforços empreendidos, não foi possível encontrar uma solução que contemplasse todas as necessidades envolvidas naquele momento, e a peça voltou a ser apresentada sem a interpretação de Libras.

A Fundação lamenta muito o ocorrido, especialmente os prejuízos causados à comunidade surda presente. O compromisso com acessibilidade é um dos pilares da instituição, que entende que cultura se faz com o acesso e o respeito a todos os públicos.

Marco Nanini foi vaiado durante espetáculo de teatro em Porto Alegre (RS) — Foto: Izabel Cristina/Arquivo pessoal

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Burnham faces climate revolt' and 'Harry wants to fix feud'
articles.summary: Several papers lead on remarks from the Duke of Sussex yesterday, where he said he hoped to reconcile with his family.
articles.body:
The Guardian says Andy Burnham will face a "climate revolt" by approving drilling at the Jackdaw gas field. The paper says that, while it will be a "major boost" for Britain's oil and gas industry, critics will argue it undermines Labour's green credentials. According to the Financial Times, ministers are expected to say that the project will help increase energy supplies this winte r. The i Paper reports that it will be able to power around a million UK homes.

The Times reports that the home secretary is facing pressure from her cabinet colleagues to water down plans which would make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK. But an ally of Shabana Mahmood tells the paper that Burnham is "on her side" and is "holding the line". "Mahmood's fight to save her migrant crackdown" is the headline.

The decision to deploy RAF jets to defend Saudi Arabia is described by the Times as an "expansion of the UK's role in the conflict in Yemen" . A defence source tells the paper that "if Houthi drones or missiles come over the border" then British jets will "take them out". The Telegraph's verdict is: "Better late than never".

The Daily Mirror leads with the Covid inquiry's findings that government failures during the pandemic allowed the virus to "spread like wildfire" in care homes. In its leader column, the paper says care home residents were "shamefully abandoned by those entrusted with protecting them".

Prince Harry's call for reconciliation with his father and brother is the focus of the Sun's front page . It says the Duke of Sussex is hoping to "fix his bitter family feud". But the Daily Mail accuses him of "reopening old wounds" in what it describes as a "new Sussex psychodrama" . Its headline reads: "Oh, do put a sock in it, Harry!".

images.caption: The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead today, according to the Guardian. The paper says the move signals Prime Minister Andy Burnham's commitment to the North Sea oil and gas industry, but "threatens to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs". It reports that the shift will be a "major boost" for Britain's oil and gas industry, and once fully operational, will account for 6% of North Sea gas production.

articles.title: Honduran illegal immigrant charged with assaulting ICE officers with hammer during New Jersey traffic stop
articles.summary: Reinieri De Jesus Licona Amador allegedly grabbed a hammer and swung it at ICE officers during a New Jersey traffic stop before being pepper sprayed.
articles.body: A Honduran national who federal authorities say was unlawfully present in the United States allegedly climbed onto his truck and repeatedly swung a hammer at Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers during a traffic stop in New Jersey this month, federal prosecutors said. Reinieri De Jesus Licona Amador, 27, was charged with assaulting federal officers and appeared Monday before U.S. Magistrate Judge Elizabeth A. Pascal in Camden federal court, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey. "Federal officers put themselves in harm’s way to enforce the law and protect the public," U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer said in a statement. "When an individual responds to a traffic stop by attacking an officer with a hammer, that conduct threatens not only the officer’s safety but the rule of law itself," he continued. "We will not allow violent attacks on federal officers to go unanswered and will hold those responsible accountable under the law." EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET Federal prosecutors said the incident began during a targeted ICE operation in Gibbsboro, when officers ran a license plate check on a truck traveling through the area. According to the criminal complaint, the vehicle was registered to Licona Amador, and a search of immigration records indicated he lacked lawful status in the United States. Officers then activated their emergency lights and pulled over Licona Amador's truck, prosecutors said. ILLEGAL ALIEN ON THE RUN AFTER ALLEGEDLY RAMMING ICE VEHICLE IN PENNSYLVANIA, PROMPTING AGENT TO FIRE WEAPON According to the complaint, as officers approached the truck, they saw Licona Amador reach into a tool container in the back seat and pick up a hammer. Prosecutors said officers ordered Licona Amador to stop moving, but he refused to comply, prompting them to open the vehicle door and attempt to remove him from the truck. He allegedly pulled away from the officers and moved to the passenger side of the truck, where they again tried unsuccessfully to restrain him. Licona Amador then climbed out of the passenger side of the truck while holding the hammer, ignoring officers' repeated commands, according to the complaint. ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SUSPECTED OF GANG TIES ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY RAMMING ICE OFFICER He allegedly climbed onto the passenger-side door and repeatedly swung the hammer at officers, prosecutors said. Officers then deployed oleoresin capsicum (OC) spray, commonly known as pepper spray, and wrestled Licona Amador to the ground, prosecutors said. articles.title: US jails Guatemalan man for 30 years over deadly smuggling operation
articles.summary: The 2022 incident resulted in the deaths of 53 migrants trapped inside a tractor-trailer in dangerously high heat.
articles.body:
A Guatemalan man has been sentenced to 30 years in a United States prison for his role in a human-smuggling operation that killed 53 migrants trapped in a truck – a disaster that had been described as one of the deadliest such incidents along the US-Mexico border in recent history.

US District Judge Orlando Garcia handed 39-year-old Rigoberto Ramon Miranda-Orozco a 30-year prison term on Tuesday, more than a year after his extradition from Guatemala in March 2025.

He was first arrested in Guatemala in August 2024, as part of a cross-border effort to dismantle the human-smuggling network.

The charges stem from a fatal incident on June 27, 2022. According to the US Department of Justice, emergency crews discovered dozens of people trapped inside an abandoned truck in a remote area on the southern outskirts of San Antonio, Texas.

A total of 64 migrants had endured a lengthy journey that began in Guatemala and continued through Mexico across the border into the US.

By the time the truck was driving from Laredo, Texas, to San Antonio – a distance of 250km (155 miles) – prosecutors say the air conditioning had stopped functioning. When the truck was discovered, temperatures were approaching 32C (90F).

Forty-eight people were pronounced dead on the scene, and five more died while receiving emergency medical treatment for heat-related illness and dehydration.

Among the dead were six children and a pregnant woman. Of those killed, 21 were Guatemalan nationals.

Miranda-Orozco has admitted to arranging travel and accommodation for two of the migrants who died in the truck and another who survived but suffered grave injuries.

He pleaded guilty in July to conspiring to bring a migrant into the US resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting the unlawful entry of migrants resulting in death and serious bodily injury.

According to The Associated Press news agency, Miranda-Orozco is among a group of nearly 20 people sentenced in the US and Guatemala in connection with the tragedy.

Felipe Orduna-Torres, identified as the leader of the operation in the US, was sentenced to life in prison in a federal court in San Antonio in June 2025.

Armando Gonzales-Ortega, described by prosecutors as Orduna-Torres’s top assistant, received an 83-year sentence.

Further proceedings remain pending, including in the case against the truck driver.

According to prosecutors, investigators found signs of passengers’ desperate attempts to escape the abandoned truck. Some had reportedly removed clothing. Scratch marks on the trailer’s interior, meanwhile, suggested that some people had clawed at the walls in a futile bid to escape.

The prosecutors said the passengers had paid as much as $15,000 for passage across the border.

“It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth,” US Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a Tuesday news conference following the sentencing.

The I-35 highway near where the truck was found runs through San Antonio from the Mexican border.

It is considered a popular smuggling corridor because of the large volume of truck traffic, Jack Staton, a former senior official with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), told the Reuters news agency at the time.

The administration of President Donald Trump has cited the need to end human trafficking as a rationale for his crackdown on irregular immigration across the southern border.

But critics have argued that hardline enforcement tactics may drive immigrants to pursue more dangerous methods for crossing the border irregularly.

articles.title: France is divided over who to blame for weekend riots
articles.summary: In France and beyond there is widespread disagreement over what led to some of the worst unrest seen in French cities in modern history.
articles.body:
"This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"

Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October.

I'd stopped Elisabeth and her friend to ask their thoughts on what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears.

"My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."

But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.

Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.

The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.

French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend.

French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black, folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.

A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left.

It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections. LFI denies this.

The mass looting of what is said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?

Emmanuel Macron, who is on his way out as president and viewed by many in France as a lame duck, and his government are accused of dropping the ball and failing to keep the country safe on Saturday.

Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.

Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts have led former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence.

Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's interior minister, Bernard Quintin, warned of the "TikTokisation" of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liège on "known far-left groups".

In France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire", said Nuñez. On Tuesday Lecornu spoke of "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups".

Previously he had accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos.

It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.

Mélenchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all.

In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students had organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians.

"Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa.

But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned."

France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday.

The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics.

Mélenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist prime minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy."

Mélenchon went on to apparently imply Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure in public finances".

France is struggling with spiralling public debt and government borrowing costs.

As for intelligence failures on Saturday, President Macron has demanded explanations and a new policing strategy. France's interior minister admitted there were not enough officers on the streets, despite the nationwide protests being publicised well in advance.

Following accusations of heavy-handedness at earlier demos, the police seemed very much out of their depth this weekend.

Of all the presidential hopefuls, it would seem Marine Le Pen of the anti-immigration National Rally party gains most politically from Saturday's shocking scenes.

She is already way ahead in opinion polls. Le Pen chose to launch a presidential-looking video address to the nation via social media on Sunday. Dressed formally, behind a large desk and in front of a French flag, she blamed Jean-Luc Mélenchon by name for his associates who "look to throw the country into chaos," she said.

She also accused the Macron government of "running out of steam", meaning that France was "taken hostage between violence and powerlessness".

She ended her video by reminding French voters they would have the opportunity to "choose a different path" in six months' time.

Le Pen's party promotes a law and order, closed-border message and, like US President Donald Trump and US Vice President JD Vance, has blamed migrants, amongst others, for the chaos in France on Saturday. French authorities have not implicated migrants in the violence.

One teacher called Mar complained that Saturday's violence "suits politicians' purpose. It distracts from weeks of legitimate protests for better public services", she said.

"Politicians aren't listening to what the students need, or what teachers need or what the French people want. They're using the violence to election-campaign to become president and to try to make their opponents look bad."

But increasing numbers in France, many amongst the young Gen Z generation, say they have dwindling faith in "the system".

That's something we see echoed in other European countries where mainly youth-led protests erupted - some violently - this weekend in Italy, Portugal and Albania as well as France and Belgium.

These demonstrations are often triggered by spiralling living costs, deteriorating public services and a sense of powerlessness people feel over their own lives.

What can we do as individuals about our rising energy costs caused by wars far away in the Middle East or in Ukraine, many ask.

Voters increasingly say they are losing faith in traditional or governing political parties to listen to concerns and address them. The young look at climate change, social inequality, impossible housing prices and AI potentially threatening their place in the job market.

According to opinion polls conducted by this year by Pew, 69% of people in France are dissatisfied with democracy. In Spain, it's 68% and in Italy, 62%. The US is experiencing similar disillusionment with 69% saying they are dissatisfied with how democracy is working.

So many people I've spoken to in France since Saturday's riots emphasise the importance in making a clear distinction between angry but peaceful protesters, and those intent on wreaking violent havoc.

Politics aside, is what we're now seeing in Europe's protest wave perhaps a powerful cocktail of a bubbling over of frustration, cries for help for the authorities to listen but also, for some, a dark sense there's little left to lose?

articles.body: NEW DELHI: CJP's Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka Tuesday approached Delhi HC challenging their judicial custody, a day before the special executive magistrate decides whether to extend their custody.The two were detained on Oct 13 after they climbed a gate to enter Jantar Mantar, which has been denotified as a protest site, to protest against SIR. Meanwhile, police have transferred the Oct 13 cases against them to Crime Branch.Das and Ranka have sought an urgent hearing, but the court is closed for Dussehra. If the executive magistrate releases them Wednesday, their petition will become redundant.However, until late Tuesday, the court’s cause list didn’t have any case listed for hearing this week. articles.title: UN experts call on India to stop using ‘excessive force’ against protesters
articles.summary: UN experts press for an ⁠independent investigation into Indian authorities’ conduct.
articles.body:
UN experts have called on the Indian government to stop the use of “excessive force” in the wake of the crackdown on opposition and student protests in India.

In a statement on Tuesday, the two dozen independent experts pressed for an impartial investigation into Indian authorities’ conduct, saying that demonstrators had sustained injuries and some reported being subjected to ill-treatment.

“Protesters have sustained injuries, with some reporting being subjected to ill-treatment. The experts expressed particular concern about reports of sexual violence and other forms of gender-based abuse in the protests and related detentions,” according to the statement.

UN experts are appointed by the UN Human Rights Council to monitor and document specific human rights crises but are independent of the organisation itself.

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), along with other opposition parties and student organisations, has led protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, after 130 million names were removed from voter lists.

The protesting groups said the removal disproportionately affected poor and homeless people as well as ethnic minorities including Muslims, who are unlikely to vote for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The BJP and India’s Election Commission deny the accusations. The Election Commission said it was removing duplicate, deceased, shifted and otherwise ineligible voters and that anyone excluded in error can pursue appeals.

“Despite the non-violent nature of the assemblies, law enforcement agencies have reportedly deployed force against unarmed students including by means of police so-called lathi charges, and have prevented thousands from joining the protests,” the UN experts said.

Lathi charges are coordinated movements by a policing force using sticks to disperse crowds.

“We call on the authorities to immediately cease the use of excessive force, rescind blanket assembly bans, and refrain from the misuse of digital surveillance, including through biometrics, and internet disruptions,” they added.

India has repeatedly dismissed such criticism and cast it as interference in the country’s internal affairs, including when the UN human rights office earlier this month expressed concerns over mass detentions in relation to the latest protests.

articles.title: ‘Now is the time to act’: UN launches initiative to tackle military AI risks
articles.summary: The United Nations is launching a new initiative to address the risks posed by the growing use of artificial intelligence in military operations, warning
articles.body: The United Nations is launching a new initiative to address the risks posed by the growing use of artificial intelligence in military operations, warning that the scope for human judgment is narrowing, including in the nuclear domain.The initiative, led by the UN Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR), is set to launch on Thursday. It will establish an international forum bringing together key stakeholders from across the world to discuss the military applications of AI and ways to address the threats associated with the technology, AP reported.Robin Geiss, head of the Geneva-based institute, warned at a UN press conference on Tuesday that “the margin for human judgment is increasingly narrow, including in the nuclear domain”.Geiss said it remained difficult to determine how close the world was to a point where machines could act beyond human control. However, he stressed that uncertainty itself was a major concern the new initiative aimed to address.AI is increasingly being integrated into military functions, including early warning systems, intelligence gathering and reconnaissance, making it difficult to identify when human control could be compromised, he said.UN warns against delaying AI safeguardsGeiss said governments had long been reluctant to address safeguards for artificial intelligence. However, the rapid spread of AI capabilities and their potential consequences have prompted a growing recognition that action is needed.“We stand at a crossroads — that now is the time to act, including on military AI,” he said.He acknowledged that global competition to lead in AI development posed significant challenges to international cooperation. However, concerns about the technology's impact were increasingly crossing geopolitical boundaries and prompting action from major powers.As an example, Geiss cited a proposal made last month for the United States and China to establish an AI safety alert system to address issues that could threaten national security.UN seeks responsible AI development in defence sectorUNIDIR established a Center of Excellence on AI, Peace and Security this summer, creating the UN's first permanent platform dedicated to these issues. Geiss said the centre had received funding from all five major nuclear powers — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France.The new military AI forum will be part of the centre's broader efforts to bring together stakeholders from different sectors and regions to address the technology's implications for global security.Alongside the military AI forum and industry-focused initiative, UNIDIR is launching an effort to address the potential misuse of artificial intelligence by armed groups.Geiss warned that such groups were already using AI to support operational planning, execution and logistics, highlighting the need to address the risks posed by the technology beyond state militaries.“The urgent issue of AI in the military domain will certainly no longer be allowed to linger in the shadows,” Geiss said, adding that the international community must work together to confront the challenges posed by military AI.You use AI every day. articles.title: Florida puts 77-year-old man to death for deputy's murder as state closes in on execution record
articles.summary: A 77-year-old Florida man was put to death in the Sunshine State's 18th execution this year as Gov. Ron DeSantis continues the state's accelerated execution pace.
articles.body: A 77-year-old Florida man was executed on Tuesday for killing a sheriff's deputy more than 40 years ago, marking the Sunshine State's 18th execution of the year as Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis continues an accelerated pace of executions. William Reaves was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke following a three-drug injection. He was convicted of first-degree murder in connection with the September 1986 shooting death of Indian River County sheriff's deputy Richard Raczkoski. Reaves said he did not have any last words. About 30 seconds after the injection began, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. A few minutes later, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and shouted his name, but the man gave no response. A medic checked for a heartbeat or other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later. FLORIDA EXECUTES INMATE WHO KILLED CELLMATE BECAUSE HE WANTED DEATH PENALTY Raczkoski's brother, Marc, told reporters after witnessing the execution that his brother finally received justice, while Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said that he viewed the execution as closure rather than justice. "Would we all be so lucky to be 77 years old and to die so peacefully," Flowers said at a press conference. "That’s not justice in any way, in my opinion." On Sept. 23, 1986, Raczkoski responded to a 911 call that Reaves had made from a payphone at a Vero Beach convenience store, according to court records. After the deputy arrived at the scene and the two men began talking, a gun fell out of Reaves’ pants, officials said. The two men struggled over the weapon before Reaves eventually regained control of it. Raczkoski was attempting to run away when Reaves shot him four times, according to investigators. He died from his wounds later that day. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court later overturned the conviction due to a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. After the second trial, Reaves was again convicted and sentenced to death, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful. The U.S. Supreme Court denied Reaves’ request for a stay of execution and petition asking the court to review his case without comment on Tuesday. TWO FLORIDA INMATES DIE IN RARE DOUBLE EXECUTION AFTER SCOTUS DENIES STAYS The state Supreme Court also rejected Reaves’ appeals last week that sought to halt the execution. His attorneys challenged Florida’s three-drug lethal injection protocol. Executions in the state are carried out through the injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld the protocol against similar challenges. Florida's method is different from the single-drug injection used in states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital and was rushed to the hospital last month. Pike has since been released from the hospital and returned to prison. Reaves' attorneys also argued that jurors who recommended the death penalty were never made aware that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs had rated the Army veteran as 100% disabled because of post-traumatic stress disorder linked to his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 military veterans appealed to DeSantis in a letter on Monday to halt the execution, pointing to those factors. Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year. Florida has accelerated its pace of executions amid a flurry of death warrants signed by DeSantis since 2025. The governor oversaw a state record 19 executions last year, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976, accounting for approximately 40% of the U.S. total of 47 executions for 2025. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Florida would tie last year's record if Jesse Guardado, 64, is put to death as scheduled on Nov. 5 for robbing and killing a woman to buy drugs in 2004. Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the country so far this year, including Reaves. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first time a state has done so in nearly a decade. DeSantis has said he wants justice for victims’ families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Woman sues popular Texas taco chain for $250K after allegedly finding cow tooth in meal, restaurant confirms
articles.summary: Nohemi Castillo claims she nearly swallowed a cow tooth in her Torchy's Tacos barbacoa, and the Austin chain confirmed the unusual object was real.
articles.body: Taco 'bout biting off more than you can chew. A Texas woman's lunch took an unexpectedly toothsome turn when she allegedly discovered a cow tooth in her taco, prompting a lawsuit against popular restaurant chain Torchy's Tacos over a bizarre ingredient the company has since confirmed was the real deal. Nohemi Castillo claims she nearly swallowed the tooth while eating takeout from the chain's South Congress Avenue location in Austin on June 9, according to a lawsuit independently obtained by Fox News Digital and filed Oct. 13 in Travis County District Court. ROACHES CAUGHT CRAWLING ACROSS POPULAR STEAKHOUSE'S KITCHEN FLOOR IN VIRAL EMPLOYEE VIDEO The order included the chain's "Democrat" tacos, according to the complaint, although a cow tooth was certainly not among the advertised ingredients. Torchy's Tacos confirmed the unusual discovery in a statement to Austin TV station KVUE, saying its own investigation determined that the object was a cow tooth. "Upon receiving the guest complaint, we conducted a thorough review and identified the item as a cow tooth," the company said. "This can occasionally happen when processing the meat, though it is quite rare." The restaurant explained that its barbacoa comes from natural beef cheek sourced from a supplier, adding that it has taken steps to prevent similar incidents. FDA WIDENS CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK INVESTIGATION TO SIX MORE STATES AS CONFIRMED CASES TOP 6,000 "We have partnered with our supplier to reinforce their internal procedures to prevent this from happening in the future," Torchy's said. Castillo's attorney, Scott Vasquez, told Fox News Digital that the company did not acknowledge to him that the object was a cow tooth until the story attracted local media attention in October, roughly four months after the incident. Vasquez provided Fox News Digital with additional photographs showing the tooth beside a tape measure, offering a closer look at the sizable object Castillo claims she nearly swallowed. Another photograph included in the court filing shows the object resting on aluminum foil beside what appears to be taco meat. A witness statement provided by Castillo's attorney describes the moment an ordinary lunch with a colleague took an unpleasant turn. THREE WENDY'S EMPLOYEES ALLEGEDLY TOOK FOOD FROM TRASH, SPAT ON IT BEFORE SERVING UNHAPPY CUSTOMER "As we were eating, I heard an ‘awww!’ When I turned to Nohemi, I saw her pulling something out of her mouth, she said, 'I think it's a bone,'" the witness wrote. The colleague described Castillo examining the object while holding her left cheek before concluding that it appeared to be a tooth. According to the lawsuit, Castillo was disgusted and sickened by the discovery and visited a doctor later that evening, where she received prescriptions. The complaint alleges that she incurred medical expenses and experienced physical pain, mental anguish and other damages. Castillo is suing Torchy's Tacos and Success Foods Management Group, which does business as Torchy's Tacos, alleging that the defendants failed to properly prepare, inspect and distribute the food before selling it to customers. The lawsuit further alleges that Torchy's failed to adequately monitor its meat supplier and breached implied warranties that food sold to consumers is fit for consumption. It also alleges violations of the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act and federal food safety requirements. Castillo contends that she would not have purchased the meal, or would have examined it more closely, had she known about the alleged defect. She is seeking monetary relief of $250,000 or less, with any final award to be determined by a jury. Vasquez also told Fox News Digital that he has become aware of other individuals reporting similar experiences with Torchy's since the story received attention, although those accounts have not been independently verified. The attorney characterized the company's earlier responses as providing limited information while shifting blame and responsibility to others. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Torchy's, meanwhile, maintains that it took the complaint seriously and conducted a thorough review. "We are aware of the situation and take all concerns about our food seriously," the company told KVUE. Torchy's did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: TSMC plans 3nm semiconductor manufacturing at second Japan factory, investment to exceed USD 23 billion
articles.summary: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) plans to manufacture advanced semiconductors using 3-nanometre (3nm) process technology at the second
articles.body: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) plans to manufacture advanced semiconductors using 3-nanometre (3nm) process technology at the second factory of its Japan subsidiary, Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing (JASM), with total equipment investment in the venture expected to exceed USD 23 billion.In a post on X, TSMC's Japan account thanked the Japanese government for its support for the second factory, saying production and investment plans would be implemented in phases based on market demand and would proceed on the premise of government support."Specific production and investment plans will be implemented in phases in response to market demand," the company said.TSMC said the facility would help it meet growing demand for advanced chips driven by artificial intelligence (AI), while providing technology to customers in Japan and other markets."Moving forward, JASM will continue to work alongside our partners to provide cutting-edge technology to customers in Japan and around the world, using innovative green manufacturing technologies that are environmentally considerate, in order to meet the strong demand in the AI era," the company said.JASM is a joint venture established by TSMC and its partners to operate semiconductor manufacturing facilities in Kumamoto, Japan. The company's second factory is part of TSMC's broader manufacturing presence in the country, with the planned use of 3nm technology marking a move towards more advanced chip production.In August, TSMC and Sony Semiconductor Solutions agreed to establish another joint venture, Advanced Vision Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp., in Kumamoto to develop and manufacture next-generation image sensors. Commercial production at the facility is scheduled to begin in 2029, according to a report by Focus Taiwan.The latest announcement comes as TSMC reports strong growth in its business amid rising demand for advanced semiconductor technologies. The company reported a 68.7 per cent year-on-year increase in net profit to USD 23.86 billion in the July-September quarter, while revenue rose 50.9 per cent to USD 46.72 billion.TSMC said the JASM investment and production plans would be carried out in stages in response to market demand, with government support remaining a condition for proceeding.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Pod Save America' hosts warn El-Sayed to tone down 'condescension' on Muslim Brotherhood questions
articles.summary: Jon Favreau and Tommy Vietor debated El-Sayed's testy response to Muslim Brotherhood questions on "Pod Save America," warning against "condescension."
articles.body: Former Obama staffers who host the "Pod Save America" podcast debated Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s handling of a recent question about his family’s alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. While Tommy Vietor and his co-hosts sympathized with El-Sayed over questions they considered "bigoted," Jon Favreau warned that El-Sayed must keep in mind that he is speaking not just to the questioner, but also to voters who may be concerned about the Muslim Brotherhood itself. Concerns about alleged ties between El-Sayed's family and the Muslim Brotherhood emerged after the Washington Free Beacon reported on social media posts in which El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, described her family's history with the organization, including her and El-Sayed's mother. At an October 17 town hall, El-Sayed bristled when an audience member asked whether he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. After disavowing the organization, El-Sayed turned the scrutiny back on the audience member, saying, "You’re asking the question because implicitly, you assume that I’ll have dual loyalties, right? You assume that I wouldn’t disavow, or that I'll have some higher order allegiance than to the Constitution, correct? Tommy, is that what you imply?" 'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS DEFEND EL-SAYED COMPARING HIMSELF TO JFK OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SCRUTINY Favreau criticized Republican attempts to tie El-Sayed to the organization through his family connections, but argued that the GOP was using the issue to sway voters. "It's somewhat smarter for them to throw out the Muslim Brotherhood thing because it's like, ‘This is a new piece of information that people might have no idea what the Muslim Brotherhood is,’" he said, appearing to frame the tactical mindset of Republican operatives. "'Sounds pretty scary, doesn't it?' 'Terrorist organization.' 'Maybe you don't know the history of the Muslim Brotherhood.' 'Maybe it's got foreign ties to Egypt and he, you know, his family, his family's from Egypt.'" "So, to respond to that, as bulls — as it is, and of course, he like knocked it down. But you've got to forget about the a--hole asking you the question," Favreau continued. "You've got to give the answer as if someone who might have a question about a Muslim Brotherhood tie is not necessarily like totally Islamophobic and like that kid or like Trump or like Mike Rogers, but like might have a question, and you don't want — and you don't want to condescend to that person or be like, ‘No, you're an a--hole for asking.’ Right?" "And I'm not saying he did," he added. "I thought it was a good — I thought he could have used like 20% less condescension in the answer." Vietor agreed that El-Sayed’s tone could have been better, and replied, "There’s a slightly more empathetic version of that." Fellow co-host Jon Lovett said, "Stop fighting with that guy and speak to the people that are not." ABDUL EL-SAYED INVOKES JFK TO DISMISS 'CRAZY' QUESTIONS OVER FAMILY'S ALLEGED TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD Favreau recalled his experience working for former President Barack Obama and said that, regardless of whether a characterization of a candidate's statements is fair, candidates and public officials have to be careful about rhetoric and tone when speaking to voters. "You can say this from the cheap seats because I am sure when you are Abdul, and you're going around doing this and there are people who are f---ing just calling into question your loyalty to your country that you love, it must f---ing infuriate you," Favreau said. "And it's not fair that what he has to do in response is to eat s--- and just give a nice answer with a smile." "But like we were there when Barack Obama had to do it, and you know Zohran Mamdani had to do it and like, unfortunately, there's a double standard, and it's unfair, but you still have to do it to win an election anyway and it f---ing sucks," he added. Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment but did not immediately receive a response. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Jesse Arm, vice president of external affairs at the Manhattan Institute and a former pollster who has followed the Michigan Senate race, suggested El-Sayed's confrontational demeanor may be a key reason he is not doing as well against his Republican opponent as the Democratic gubernatorial nominee is doing in her race in Michigan. "The ‘Pod Save America’ guys are partisan hacks who bend over backward to excuse El-Sayed’s radicalism and dismiss legitimate scrutiny as bigotry. But even they recognize that his nastiness and condescension are deeply off-putting," Arm told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And if even his most sympathetic defenders can see it, imagine how he comes across to ordinary Michigan voters," he added. "This is a big part of the reason he’s poised to dramatically underperform the state’s Democratic gubernatorial nominee."

articles.title: Portugal cost-of-living protesters pour back into camps cleared by police
articles.summary: Police arrested 55 people while clearing protest camps in Lisbon and Porto.
articles.body:
Thousands of protesters have returned to two central squares in Portugal for demonstrations against an intensifying housing crisis, hours after police cleared their camps in the capital, Lisbon, and the city of Porto, arresting 55 people.

Activists have demanded the centre-right government withdraw a bill that makes evictions easier and ends rent caps on new leases, which passed a first parliamentary reading.

The demonstrators in Lisbon sought to rebuild their sit-in camp at Rossio Square on Tuesday, while those in Porto were returning to the northern city’s Dom Joao I Square.

Organisers said more than 1,000 people had gathered at each square. Activists have occupied Lisbon’s Rossio Square since Saturday, pitching around 200 tents, and Porto’s Dom Joao I Square for around 10 days.

Debora Miranda, 41, a communications consultant, told Reuters she joined the Rossio Square protest to represent generations struggling with soaring costs. “If people don’t feel at home, in every sense of the word, they can’t move forward with their lives…enough is enough.”

The camps mirrored housing protests in neighbouring Spain , and coincided with unrest over rising living costs in countries such as France , Belgium and Italy .

Shortly before 6am, after warning protesters that the camps were illegal, police launched coordinated operations in both cities. Demonstrators in Porto followed orders and dismantled their own tents. Officers cleared Lisbon’s Rossio Square in what Carla Valadao, a spokesperson for the camp, described as “very aggressive”.

Public Security Police superintendent Sergio Soares told reporters that the eviction had been “calm, proportionate and appropriate, with no police charge”.

The 55 detainees were later released pending a court appearance in Lisbon on Wednesday.

Portugal is grappling with one of Europe’s worst housing affordability crises as purchase prices have more than doubled since 2017 and rents for new leases have nearly doubled.

Jorge Paixao, 19, a history student, called it “a societal crisis”, saying his generation needed “the ability to live with dignity, start families and rejuvenate Portugal”.

The squeeze is most acute in the major cities, where there has also been opposition to excessive tourism and an influx of so-called digital nomads, people who travel while working remotely.

articles.title: Lane Kiffin is already getting his excuses ready for LSU's disappointing regular season
articles.summary: With two losses and a brutal remaining schedule, Lane Kiffin is already building his excuses for LSU's College Football Playoff hopes fading.
articles.body: Find yourself something or someone you love as much as Lane Kiffin loves making excuses for things that haven't even happened yet. Kiffin's first season as head coach of the LSU Tigers has been a bit of a roller coaster. They've at times looked dominant, like the opening weekend demolition of Clemson, then struggled in a loss to what should have been an overmatched Kentucky team. The loss at Ole Miss, in a highly charged, emotional return to Oxford was understandable on the face of it, and yet was exactly the type of game Kiffin was hired to win. Now, with two losses in the first seven games, LSU still has a tough schedule remaining. The Tigers have upcoming games against Auburn on the road this weekend, a home game against Alabama, followed by Texas in Baton Rouge, a road game against Tennessee, and a season-ending trip to Arkansas. For a program that entered the season with aspirations of reaching the College Football Playoff, Kiffin needs to win out to feel good about finishing in playoff position. LANE KIFFIN IS ALREADY SOMEHOW BLAMING THE SEC'S NEW CONFERENCE SCHEDULE FOR LSU'S INJURIES And he's already got his excuses ready for if they don't. In a news conference this week, Kiffin explained to reporters that he opposed the SEC's new nine-game conference schedule, and detailed how the math guarantees the SEC an additional eight in-conference losses. "And they kinda said when it was proposed, they said, 'Well, okay, you're going to take on eight more losses. I mean, that's going to be real, there's no way of changing the math, that's going to happen. So you see that, I think somebody said there's two SEC teams in the top-10 right now, and I said before it started, I said, 'Take away the first SEC game that you play because that's going to be brand new, the ninth one came early and got added and replaced an early win, you know where's that going to put you?' "Look at this team [Auburn Tigers], if you took away their first SEC loss, and it was just a win versus a Group of Six team, they'd be a top-10 team right now. They'd have one loss, on the road at Tennessee to a really good team. And somehow now, because of adding an extra game, they're not even ranked and they just beat the number one team in the country." He concluded the answer, "It's just where football is, and they can't see like they do in basketball or baseball, metrics, so it is what it is." articles.title: No phone checks or internet jammers, yet no one was on their phone or cheating': Indian student moves to US, says exams there are ‘biggest cultural shock’
articles.summary: If you've studied in India, you probably know what an exam hall looks like.
articles.body: If you've studied in India, you probably know what an exam hall looks like. Someone is watching the room, phones are strictly off-limits, and even turning around to look at a friend can get you into trouble.Now imagine sitting for an exam without an invigilator walking around or someone checking whether you're using your phone. Sounds unusual, right?That's what caught an Indian student's attention after moving to the US. Just two months into their stay, the student shared their experience on X (formerly Twitter), saying the biggest cultural shock so far had been the way exams were conducted."It's been 2 months since I landed in the US, and my biggest cultural shock has been exam ethics," they wrote.The student described exams where there were no invigilators, books were allowed, and nobody was checking phones or using internet jammers. What surprised them most was that, according to their observation, nobody seemed to be cheating or looking at their phones."Cutthroat competition in India just doesn't allow for this kind of trust," they added.The post got people talking. Some understood exactly what the student meant, while others pointed out that exams in the US aren't always so relaxed.‘We're just not used to this in India’Anyone who's prepared for a competitive exam in India knows how stressful it can get. There's pressure to score well, the constant comparison with other students and, for many, the feeling that one result could affect their future.And that pressure doesn't end with school. College exams, entrance tests and job-related assessments can all come with their own set of expectations.So, when a student used to strict supervision finds themselves in an exam where they're trusted to follow the rules, it's understandable that they'd notice the difference.That seems to be what happened here. The student wasn't just surprised by open-book exams. They were surprised by the apparent lack of monitoring and the fact that, in their experience, students weren't taking advantage of it.Of course, this doesn't mean every university in the US works this way. Exam rules vary, and plenty of American colleges have strict supervision and restrictions on phones.But the post has got people asking a question that goes beyond exam rules: does the pressure to score well change the way students behave?Other students say it's not always like thisNot everyone agreed with the student's description of American universities.One person, who said they also study at a university in the US, pointed out that invigilators are present for some exams and that not every test allows students to use books or notes."I also go to an American university, and it's not always like this for every class; there are invigilators, and not all tests are open book," the user wrote.They also warned that students caught cheating could face serious consequences.Another commenter agreed that some exams in the US might be more relaxed but disagreed with the idea that competition was necessarily less intense."While I agree exams are far more relaxed here, it's not in the way you're describing," they wrote.And that's worth keeping in mind. One student's experience at their university doesn't tell us how exams work across an entire country. Some students may have open-book tests with little supervision, while others sit through closely monitored exams just as they would in India.Does the pressure to get good marks make a difference?One response to the post focused on something many Indian students will recognise: the pressure to stay ahead of everyone else."The trust isn't the shock; it's that nobody there sees a reason to cheat," one user commented.The person suggested that some students feel tempted to cheat when they believe others are doing it and worry that being honest could put them at a disadvantage.That's a strong generalisation, and it certainly doesn't describe every student in India. Many students work hard and take their academic honesty seriously.Still, the pressure to score well is real for many young people. Getting into a particular college, securing a scholarship or qualifying for a competitive exam can feel like a lot rests on a single result.When marks become the main measure of success, students can end up worrying more about their scores than about what they've actually learnt.That doesn't justify cheating. But it does raise a fair question about how much pressure students are expected to handle and whether the focus on marks sometimes goes too far.Cheating can have serious consequences in the US, tooSome people responding to the post also pointed out that American universities aren't casual about cheating.Students who break academic integrity rules can face disciplinary action. Depending on the university and the offence, the consequences may include a failing grade, suspension or expulsion.And an open-book exam doesn't mean anything goes. Students may be allowed to consult their notes but still be prohibited from using their phones, searching the internet or sharing answers.So, fewer visible checks don't necessarily mean fewer rules. The student was describing what they had seen, not claiming that cheating never happens in the US.One post, two very different experiencesThe discussion comes down to something fairly simple: how much responsibility should students be given during exams?Some people believe close supervision is needed to keep things fair. Others feel students should be trusted to do their own work and face the consequences if they don't.Neither approach guarantees that everyone will behave honestly. An invigilator can't catch everything, and a room without one doesn't automatically mean students will cheat.But the student's experience has clearly struck a nerve, particularly among people familiar with the pressure of exams in India.After just two months in the US, they found the approach to exams surprising enough to call it their biggest cultural shock so far.And while people may disagree about whether their experience is typical, the responses show that the relationship between competition, trust and academic honesty is something students have strong feelings about.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates.
