articles.title: Australian lawmaker loses both legs in vehicle attack as suspect appears in court
articles.summary: Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said Wednesday, as the man accused of the attack appeared in court.
articles.body: SYDNEY — Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said Wednesday, as the man accused of the attack appeared in court. Doctors amputated Haines’ left leg after the alleged attacker struck her twice with his car in Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne, on Monday, Phil Haines said. They worked for days to save her right leg but were ultimately unsuccessful, he told a news conference in Melbourne. “The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family,” he said. Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old resident of the rural town of Tarrawingee within Haines’ electorate, was charged with three offenses: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a public official. Additional charges of cannabis cultivation and possession have also been laid against Nugent, court filings showed. The suspect was restrained by members of the public at the scene before being arrested. Haines, an independent lawmaker who has championed causes including climate change and regional housing, remains in critical condition. Police are still investigating the motive for the rare attack on an elected official. During a brief court appearance Wednesday, Nugent’s lawyer said his client suffers from a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and was also being treated for concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. His lawyer told the magistrate his client had some mental health concerns and that it was his first time in custody. There was no application for bail, and the case was deferred until Feb. 4. Anti-terrorism police are among the agencies investigating the incident. While police allege the attack was “targeted,” they believe it was an isolated incident. There was no intelligence to suggest any threat to Haines, and the Australian Federal Police received no warning of any imminent danger from the alleged attacker, Commissioner Krissy Barrett told reporters. “What I can say is we didn’t have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” she said. Victoria state police said they could not find any direct past contact between Haines and Nugent, with the motive still unknown. “Motivation is one of these things that we absolutely need to explore. His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centerpiece of the investigation,” Victoria Police Chief Mike Bush said. Bush declined to comment on the man’s mental health, saying the matter was before the court. Haines had worked in nursing, midwifery and academia before being elected to parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in both 2022 and 2025. Violent attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, where federal lawmakers, state leaders and even prime ministers are often seen shopping, grabbing coffee or attending community events with relatively little security. However, concerns about politicians’ safety have grown in recent years amid rising political polarization, online abuse and threats against elected officials, prompting calls for greater protections while preserving the accessibility that has long characterized Australian politics.

articles.title: China defends DeepSeek after U.S. ban of its AI from government systems
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security said federal civilian agencies should remove the Chinese startup’s products from their IT systems, citing security concerns.
articles.body: HONG KONG — China hit back Tuesday at a U.S. ban on the use of Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek’s products by federal civilian agencies and warned of retaliatory measures as the two AI powers race to develop the technology. The Department of Homeland Security said the agencies should remove DeepSeek products as well as third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek from their IT systems, according to a notice made public Monday. The latest warnings reflect “the depth of strategic distrust between Beijing and Washington” even as U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping work hard to keep their personal relationship “warm and constructive,” said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at the Washington-based Asia Group consultancy. The Homeland Security order, dating back to late July, also blocks civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. DeepSeek’s open-source models are widely available in countries including the United States, and are mostly free to use. The notice in the Federal Register alleges that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors.” Concerns include that DeepSeek’s servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data, the order says. Asked in Beijing about the U.S. ban, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies.” “China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security,” she told reporters. China’s Ministry of Commerce also expressed “strong dissatisfaction and firm opposition” in response to the U.S. move, saying late Tuesday that the U.S. side disregarded the consensus reached between Xi and Trump and ignored the broader landscape of China-U.S. economic and trade relations. Through discriminatory restrictions under “the guise of national security,” the U.S. is trying to suppress and contain China, the commerce ministry statement said. “China will closely monitor the situation and take all necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.” DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment. China and the U.S. have recently made progress in some collaboration on AI governance, including a U.S. proposal for setting up a notification system on national security-related incidents, but they remain at odds on many issues. AI is expected to be on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet again in mid-November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. The two leaders last met in September as Xi made a state visit to Washington. U.S.-led restrictions still ban China from accessing some of the world’s most advanced AI chips and the machines that make them. The U.S. also has said Chinese AI startups including DeepSeek have engaged in large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American AI models, claims that Beijing has dismissed. Last week, Beijing rolled out its own proposals to restrict exports of certain advanced AI models.

articles.summary: Qualcomm is reportedly planning to lay off some of its employees globally.
articles.body: Qualcomm is reportedly planning to lay off some of its employees globally. According to a Reuters report, the job cuts are part of a "performance-focused reduction" following the annual employee reviews. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon has sent a memo to the staff, informing them of ‌notifications beginning in November. As stated in the report, CEO Amon said in the memo that the job cuts are part of an effort to build "a stronger performance culture" and address situations where the company "has consistently fallen short of expectations".Qualcomm has about 52,000 employees globally as of September last year. The memo, however, did not reveal the number of employees that will be affected by the layoffs.Amon said the job cuts would be based on the company’s business priorities, organisational needs, and the skills and expertise required."As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies ⁠and skills ​we require," Critiano Amon wrote. "We must have the right ​people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue ​to succeed."Impact of rising memory priceQualcomm is one of the world's biggest smartphone chipmakers. It has been hit this year by a slump in consumer electronics sales as rising memory prices impacted demand in key markets. The company’s shares have risen just 1.5% in 2026, compared with gains of more than ​12% for the benchmark S&P 500 and nearly 60% for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index.Qualcomm released its latest earnings report earlier this year in July. The company then forecasted quarterly profit below estimates and said revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected. However, it then signalled that growth in data-center and ​other non-handset businesses would ​more than offset ⁠the lost revenue by fiscal 2027. articles.title: FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing’s long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
articles.summary: Boeing has struggled to restore its reputation after two deadly crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off Indonesia and in Ethiopia.
articles.body: Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines. The Federal Aviation Administration approved the Max 10 for passenger service Tuesday, ending years of delays. The 737 Max 10’s certification represents another milestone in Boeing’s efforts to restore its reputation and financial footing after years of safety, quality and production challenges. With production approved, the aircraft can now be sold to domestic and foreign carriers. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the certification followed “extensive safety reviews,” including thousands of hours of test flights, and called it a major win for American manufacturing. “To think that it took us almost 10 years to get here. We all probably had a little less gray hair 10 years ago,” Duffy said during a visit Tuesday to Boeing’s manufacturing plant in Everett, Washington. The Max 10 is an important piece of the company’s effort to regain ground in the narrow-body market. For airlines, the larger plane offers a way to carry more passengers on a single flight, potentially lowering costs per seat. For travelers, it could eventually mean more seats on popular routes, though the impact on fares will depend on how airlines deploy the planes and how much competition they face. Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said during Duffy’s visit that the certification “clears the path to deliver an airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation.” The Max 10 will typically seat 185-210 passengers, according to Boeing, compared with 175-195 on the Max 9 and 160-180 on the Max 8. “Today is a very, very special day. It caps years of hard work and dedication by many,” Pope said. “It marks another major milestone in our recovery, and it unlocks a key to our future growth.” The company expects to begin deliveries in 2027. The single-aisle jet was introduced at the Paris Air Show in 2017 to help Boeing compete with rival Airbus. But technical and regulatory hurdles repeatedly delayed certification. Boeing’s struggles have been particularly acute since two deadly crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia. In 2024, a panel flew off an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in midair, renewing scrutiny of Boeing’s manufacturing and safety practices. The delays have held up a key part of Boeing’s business. More than 30 customers worldwide have ordered 1,555 Max 10s that Boeing has yet to deliver, accounting for more than 30% of its total 737 Max backlog. Major customers include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Ryanair. Alaska Airlines joined that list in January, ordering 105 Max 10s, with options for 35 more. The Max 10 is intended to compete with Airbus’ A321neo model family, which entered service in 2017. The largest A321neo can carry more passengers and fly farther without refueling than the Max 10. Still, Boeing designed the Max 10 to carry more passengers while burning less fuel than older aircraft — a potentially attractive combination for airlines facing soaring jet fuel costs amid the U.S. war with Iran. Those rising costs have put added pressure on airlines to control expenses. Certification means the FAA has determined that the Max 10’s design meets safety standards, following engineering reviews and flight testing. But Boeing must continue to show it can consistently build the aircraft to the approved design, and each plane must be cleared before it can fly passengers. The Max 10’s certification completes the lineup of four 737 Max models. The FAA cleared the Max 7 for airline operations in August. Pope on Tuesday described the certification of both the Max 7 and Max 10 in the same year as a sign of the company’s resilience. In the wake of the fatal Max 8 crashes, the FAA overhauled how it certifies Boeing aircraft. But over the past 18 months, the agency has gradually eased some of its restrictions on the company, increasing the limit on how many planes Boeing can produce. In July, the FAA also said Boeing could once again issue airworthiness certificates for its 737 Max and 787 planes at the end of production, allowing the company to take back some responsibility for determining whether finished aircraft are ready to fly.

articles.title: Texas couple charged in shooting death of Missouri high schooler on her way to the zoo
articles.summary: Alyssa Wilson was driving to the St. Louis Zoo for Halloween-themed festivities when she was attacked. Authorities said she had no connection to the suspects.
articles.body: A couple from Texas were charged this week in the deadly freeway shooting of a 17-year-old high school girl who was driving to the zoo for a Halloween celebration. The St. Louis County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office in Missouri charged Willie Herndon, 42, with first-degree murder and armed criminal action in connection with last week’s attack, which killed Alyssa Wilson, authorities said Monday. Taiya Herndon, who investigators said is his wife, is charged with hindering prosecution, accused of driving her husband to an Illinois hotel 12 miles from St. Louis, prosecuting attorney Melissa Price Smith said at a news conference Monday. It’s not clear whether either of the two, from Arlington, Texas, has a lawyer. The state public defender’s office for the area did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The attack killed Alyssa, who was on the precipice of adulthood and optimistic about the journey ahead, her father, Robert Hickman, said at the news conference. “Alyssa was 17, excited about her life, excited about her future,” he said as he teared up. The shooting occurred around 7 p.m. Wednesday, when Alyssa was driving south on Interstate 170 in Overland, Missouri, just northwest of St. Louis, said Jack Abell, chief deputy commander of the region’s Major Case Squad. She was on her way to Halloween festivities at the St. Louis Zoo, known as “Boo at the Zoo,” Abell said. According to security video, Alyssa was traveling south and had just passed a white Buick Enclave that was stopped on the shoulder when the sound of a single round was heard, Abell said at the news conference. “A person exited the vehicle and stood outside for a short period of time,” he said. “There was a gunshot, got back in the vehicle. The vehicle turned its hazards off and continued on.” The round went through the rear of the red Buick Encore that Alyssa was driving, Abell said. First responders found Alyssa with a gunshot wound, he said. She was rushed to Barnes-Jewish Hospital in St. Louis, where she was pronounced dead. The Herndons had no connection to the girl, Abell said. Wilson was 60 days from turning 18, said Hickman, her father. “We were getting ready to take our first family vacation together to go to Disney for her to see her favorite person in the world, Princess Tiana,” he said, referring to the character from the animated movie “The Princess and the Frog.” “Unfortunately, she’s not going to get to do that anymore,” Hickman said. “This was a senseless act.” The couple were found after investigators used security video of the shooting, as well as automated license plate readers, to track that Buick, which had an out-of-state registration, Abell said. The vehicle was under surveillance for “long hours” before investigators saw the couple come out of the hotel in Caseyville, where they were taken into custody Friday, he said. A judge-approved search in Illinois turned up a gun, as well as “supporting evidence,” Abell said, and investigators were analyzing a shell casing found alongside the freeway in Overland. Major Crimes Unit investigators interviewed Willie Herndon, he said, and came away with a better understanding of the crime. “During the interview, Willie Herndon provided details regarding his involvement in the incident and additional information pertaining to possible ongoing investigations in other areas,” Abell said. “Those investigations are continuing as we speak.” The region’s top prosecutor, Price Smith, said charges were filed in Missouri on Friday. Bail in those cases was set at $1 million for Willie Herndon and $500,000 for Taiya Herndon, to be posted in full, the Major Case Squad said in a statement. The two were being held as prosecutors await extradition to Missouri, authorities said. Inmate records for the St. Clair County Jail in Illinois show Taiya Herndon is being held on an out-of-state warrant with no bail. The records say she was booked Saturday. No jail records for Willie Herndon were available. Alongside 20 or so Major Crimes Unit investigators, the case received help from law enforcement far and wide, authorities said. “The case was solved within 36 hours due to the collaborative efforts of the FBI, ATF and the many law enforcement agencies that are in this room,” FBI St. Louis Assistant Special Agent in Charge Dave Herr said at Monday’s news conference. Abell said he could not discuss a possible motive because cases that may be connected to the attack were still under investigation.

articles.title: Australian businessman left his $29.5 million estate to his daughter, excluding his son and granddaughters; one granddaughter later won a $2.55 million court award
articles.summary: An Australian businessman left his $29.59 million estate to his daughter under his final will, making no provision for his son or granddaughters.
articles.body: An Australian businessman left his $29.59 million estate to his daughter under his final will, making no provision for his son or granddaughters. After his death in January 2022, his granddaughter Natalie Angius applied to the Supreme Court of New South Wales for family provision, arguing that she had been partly dependent on him and had not been adequately provided for. In August 2024, the court awarded Natalie $2.55 million from her grandfather’s estate. His daughter, Jenny Angius, appealed the decision, challenging Natalie’s eligibility, the circumstances warranting her claim and the size of the award. On May 27, 2025, the New South Wales Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, leaving the award in place.The 2012 will and the decision to leave the estate to his daughterJohn Angius’s final will, dated April 21, 2021, named his daughter Jenny as executor and sole beneficiary. His son Robert and Robert’s daughters, including Natalie, were not provided for under that will. An earlier will, signed on September 14, 2012, had made provision for several family members. It included indexed legacies of $200,000 for Natalie and certain other grandchildren. The earlier will was subsequently replaced by the 2021 document, and the court did not enforce its legacy in Natalie’s favour. Her eventual award arose from a separate family-provision claim under New South Wales law.Natalie told the court that John had described the 2021 will as temporary and had spoken about making further provision for his grandchildren. Evidence considered by the court included a meeting on December 20, 2021, when John gave a solicitor instructions concerning an enduring power of attorney and an enduring guardianship. The documents were not signed before his death. The first-instance judge also considered evidence of John’s statements about providing for his grandchildren. Those statements formed part of the broader assessment of his intentions, alongside the terms of his wills and the circumstances of Natalie’s relationship with him.Why Natalie qualified for family provisionNatalie brought her claim under the Succession Act 2006 (NSW). The legislation allows eligible people to seek provision from a deceased person’s estate when the will has not made adequate provision for their proper maintenance, education or advancement in life. A grandchild does not automatically qualify simply because of the family relationship. Under section 57, Natalie had to establish that she met the relevant eligibility requirements, including that she had been wholly or partly dependent on John at some point. She also had to establish the factors warranting her application under section 59. The court considers the matters listed in section 60 when deciding whether to make a provision order and determining its amount.In Le v Angius; Angius v Angius [2024] NSWSC 924, Justice Richmond found that Natalie had been partly dependent on her grandfather during her childhood and adulthood. The court considered their relationship, his financial assistance, her circumstances and the evidence of their contact, particularly in the later years of his life.Natalie was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2014. The court considered evidence that John continued to provide financial assistance and that their relationship involved regular visits, meals, care and practical support. It also examined her financial position and future needs, including the prospect of ongoing medical and personal-care expenses. The judge concluded that the absence of provision for Natalie in the 2021 will was inadequate in the circumstances. The decision was based on the evidence and the statutory test for family provision, rather than on any claim that the superseded 2012 will remained legally enforceable.How the court calculated the $2.55 million awardNatalie’s proposed provision included $950,000 for a suitably modified apartment, $100,000 for a modified vehicle and an additional sum to provide a financial buffer and income for future medical and care needs. The judge assessed the amount required for that buffer at $1.5 million. Together, the apartment, vehicle and buffer figures totalled $2.55 million, which became the lump-sum family-provision award.The court did not require the estate to meet every expense Natalie had identified. Instead, it assessed what provision was appropriate in light of her circumstances, her likely future needs, the size of the estate, her relationship with John and the other relevant statutory considerations. The award was not a payment of the $200,000 legacy in the earlier will, nor was it calculated simply by applying that earlier provision. It was a new order made under family-provision law after the court considered the evidence.Court of Appeal dismisses Jenny’s challengeJenny appealed the first-instance decision, disputing the findings concerning Natalie’s eligibility, the factors warranting her application and the amount awarded. In Angius v Angius [2025] NSWCA 113, the New South Wales Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. The court upheld the primary judge’s conclusion that Natalie was eligible to apply because she had been partly dependent on John as an adult. It also rejected the challenges to the finding that there were factors warranting her application and to the amount of provision ordered.The dismissal left Natalie’s $2.55 million award in place. The outcome demonstrates that, under New South Wales succession law, a grandchild who was not provided for in a deceased person’s final will may still seek family provision if the statutory requirements are met. Eligibility and the amount awarded depend on the evidence and the circumstances of the individual case. The case also illustrates the distinction between a will’s terms and a family-provision order. The court did not restore the earlier will or enforce its $200,000 legacy. It made a separate award after assessing Natalie’s dependency, relationship with her grandfather, financial circumstances and future needs.(Disclaimer: This article provides general information about a court decision and is not legal advice.)You use AI every day. articles.title: Huge tunnel proposed to tackle sewage blighting Lake Windermere
articles.summary: The plan would eliminate sewage spills into Windermere, blamed for turning the water green.
articles.body:
A £3.6bn proposal to stop sewage being discharged into Windermere, England's largest lake, has been unveiled.

The plans, which are backed by the local water company United Utilities and clean water campaigners, would see a tunnel up to 12 miles (19km) long built to transport sewage away from the lake.

At the moment both raw sewage and treated effluent are discharged into Windermere and campaigners say that is why parts of the lake have been turning green each summer, so-called algal blooming.

It is now up to the government to decide if the plan can be further developed, and if the £3.6bn price-tag is acceptable.

The Lake District is a Unesco World Heritage site and attracts close to 18m visitors each year.

Windermere is at its heart, with the lake holding around 300bn litres of water. That is so big that it can take 9 months for water entering one end to reach the other.

Louise Beardmore, chief executive of United Utilities, told the BBC the proposals were a "100 year solution for this lake".

"In the UK we invest in five year periods and so we come along all the time and we do a bit, then we go away and we come back and do a bit more. This is saying we need to do something differently," she said.

Beardmore said she was excited that a broad coalition including her company, regulators, the local authorities and environmental campaigners had come together to draft this proposal which is called "Only Rainwater into Windermere" (ORiW).

Perhaps the unlikeliest member of the group is activist Matt Staniek. He called today's proposal a "milestone".

"For me this is a plan on a piece of paper. It is not definitive action and that's what I want to see." he said. "This is the beginning, and the end of this is the moment that sewage stops entering Windermere."

It will now be up to the government to decide whether the plans are developed further, and if so how.

At present the sewage network around Windermere is fragmented, with homes served by a mix of public wastewater treatment works and privately owned treatment facilities and septic tanks.

When treatment works are overwhelmed, such as during heavy rain, they spill raw sewage. The rest of the time they emit a continuous stream of treated effluent which, while cleaner than raw sewage, can contain high nutrient levels.

On several occasions in the last five years the high nutrient levels and warm temperatures have combined to cause algal blooming turning parts of the lake a lurid green.

The ORiW proposal would see 12,800 people connected to the sewage network for the first time with up to 86 miles (138km) of new sewage infrastructure and a single wastewater treatment works built to serve them at the end of a 4m-wide sewage tunnel.

Two slightly different plans are being put forward. Both have the tunnel at their heart but one would see the treated effluent discharged into the River Leven, the other into the Irish Sea at Ulverston.

The report highlights two options for paying for the project.

One would see the cost passed on to United Utilities' customers and would -depending on the route chosen - add up to £3.17 to their monthly bills.

People like Nigel Wilkinson from Love Windermere group, which is linked to many local businesses, would like the cost to be spread nationally, increasing all bills in England by up to 35p a month.

"We believe Windermere is of such national significance and international significance that it is justifiable to treat this as a national asset and fund it accordingly," he says.

Much now depends on the government's enthusiasm for following through on promise made then Environment secretary Steve Reed in March 2025 to stop all sewage going into Windermere.

"We share the public's determination to protect this iconic lake." a Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs spokesperson said, stressing that further work needed to be done to test alternative options.

articles.title: Lawyer caught by BBC offering to make illegal-worker fine go away
articles.summary: Because of our investigation, the home secretary has ordered a review of how fines are issued and collected.
articles.body:
A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a £45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine, if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

At least £150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures obtained by the BBC.

In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

In a statement, she said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

Many business owners do not take the fines seriously, a law enforcement official has told us anonymously.

She told us she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth £40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

When she had asked a member of staff if the business owners intended to pay, she said she had been told: "'It's got nothing to do with me.'"

Alias came to our attention during a wider BBC probe into illegal working and criminality linked to some High Street businesses, including mini-marts and barbershops.

His name was mentioned in social media videos, including on Kurdish Facebook pages, where business owners in the UK praised his ability to resolve problems linked to immigration fines.

For months we monitored these videos, which carried Alias's name, that of his law firm, Liberty Solicitors, and a mobile phone number. Some had more than 20,000 views.

In one, a Kurdish-speaking shop owner explained that, after having been issued with a penalty for employing an illegal worker, he had "tried two or three different places to get it sorted but nobody could resolve it".

He went on to say that "Mr Alias" had got the fine cancelled - showing a letter as evidence.

Alias told the BBC he had not commissioned, paid for, approved or circulated videos on social media.

Our reporter contacted Alias on the phone, claiming to be a business owner who faced a fine after immigration officers had found somebody working at his mini-mart illegally.

There was no actual shop, worker, or fine.

During the call, which we recorded, Alias told our reporter his services would cost 10% of the fine - in this case, £4,500 - and he would want money up front.

Alias explained how liability for the fine could be shifted to somebody outside the UK, if that person could be named as owner of the business.

"Do you have anybody's name who we can use? Anybody who's gone back to Iraq, gone back to Iran?" he asked.

He then offered a fictitious example: "Say we put forward Karwan, yeah? Then fine come on Karwan's name. Karwan not here, Karwan in Iraq."

What Alias appeared to be proposing was the use of a "ghost director" - in other words, someone who is paid to put their name on official documents, thereby masking the real owner of a business.

Using ghost directors is a widespread illegal practice, the law enforcement official told us.

Bryony Rest, a senior immigration lawyer who listened to the recorded conversation, said it was "quite appalling" that a solicitor would appear to suggest a false name for the business owner.

Our reporter told Alias that to mask the real owners of the mini-mart, other people had been paid to put their names on its lease and utility bills.

The solicitor sounded encouraged by this news. "OK, fine," he said. "Then I think we should be able to find a way out of this."

An employer in the UK, who hires a worker with no legal right to work, faces being fined.

In 2024, the maximum penalty for knowingly employing illegal workers rose from £15,000 to £60,000.

A total of 5,755 fines were issued for illegal working between 2021-2025, the Home Office has told us. These would have been worth a total of £215m, but only £60.5m has been collected.

The Home Office points out that not all fines issued in the past five years would have been paid during the same time period, and the amount collected would always be lower than the value of the fines, because of appeals or discounts for fast payment.

Fitted with a secret camera, our reporter went to Alias's office in Bradford with £250 as an upfront payment.

Alias seemed annoyed, having originally asked for £500, and made a show of counting out the notes, but did not provide a receipt.

Our reporter had by this time told Alias he had found someone in the Kurdish Region of Iraq ready to declare they were the owner of the mini-mart business.

From Alias's office, the reporter rang this supposed contact, a man who gave his name as Saman. In reality, Saman was another BBC undercover journalist based in the UK.

As a solicitor, Alias could only ethically argue the case for transferring the fine if Saman were to declare to him, either verbally or in writing, that he was the real owner of the business.

In our secret recording of their conversation, Alias repeatedly asks Saman to confirm this, despite knowing there is a question mark over the mini-mart's true ownership.

Alias's frustration appears to mount with each attempt.

Alias: "Am I right in thinking that you are the owner of the shop and I'm going to write to them explaining that you're the owner of the shop?"

Saman: "I'm not the owner of the shop, but I'm ready to transfer it to my name."

Alias: "OK, but I'm going to be writing to them [the authorities] to explain that you're the owner of the shop."

Saman: "I am happy to do that yeah but also you do know, I am not the owner of the shop? And I've not even seen this shop before!"

Alias: "If you're saying that to me, then I can't do that. You understand? I can only do it if you're telling me, you are the owner of the shop."

Alias then tries to reassure Saman, telling him: "They might say, 'OK, you have to pay this money.' We don't pay the money. That's the end of it. Case finished."

Asked if he has handled similar cases, Alias tells Saman he does it "all the time for people who get fines".

We showed our recordings to Bryony Rest, who described Alias's conduct as amounting to "perverting the course of justice", and said he should be struck off.

She also noticed from the recording that, late in his meeting with the two reporters, Alias's manner suddenly changed, as if he had become suspicious.

"I can't advance an untruthful or dishonest... version of events," he is heard saying, before telling the men to decide among themselves who owns the shop.

However, Rest noted that it had been Alias himself who originally suggested "the untruthful version of events".

Later, Alias sent the undercover reporter a series of messages appearing to withdraw his offer of help.

In a subsequent phone call, he repeated that he would not pursue an untruthful claim and said he would arrange for the £250 down payment to be repaid.

The money has still not been returned, but Alias says Liberty Solicitors has made numerous attempts to return the cash.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told us the new review into the illegal-working fines scheme would aim "to ensure we are able to respond to non-compliance and non-payment through all available means".

Alias has denied ever advising anyone to put a penalty into the name of someone who was not responsible for a business, or to give false information to the Home Office, and said he never would.

"My work is to challenge penalties lawfully, through the routes Parliament has provided, usually on the basis that the person found was not an employee at all," Alias told the BBC.

He added that when our reporter proposed putting his business into someone else's name, Alias had told him in writing he could not advance an untruthful or dishonest case and did not act for him.

articles.title: Record UK wildfires spark call for firefighting aircraft
articles.summary: MPs say the UK needs firefighting aircraft, tougher prevention measures and a new wildfire strategy.
articles.body:
Record wildfires that destroyed homes, scorched thousands of hectares of countryside and stretched fire crews across the UK exposed weaknesses in preparedness, a committee of MPs has warned.

The Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said firefighting aircraft, disposable barbecue restrictions and a public awareness campaign were needed to tackle rising wildfire risk.

The report follows this year's severe wildfire season, including fires that prompted military deployment in south Wales, destroyed 19 homes in Stourbridge and scorched land in the Cairngorms, Staffordshire and Suffolk.

The government said improving wildfire preparedness was a "major priority".

A report by the cross-party committee said fires could no longer be regarded as rare or exceptional events, warning that climate change was increasing both their frequency and severity.

It said wildfire should now be treated as part of the UK's long-term climate resilience challenge, with better preparation needed for future fire seasons.

Fire and rescue services in England and Wales responded to 1,132 wildfires between 1 January and 16 August, more than the total number recorded during the whole of 2025.

During the August heatwave, millions of people across England and Wales received an emergency phone alert warning of a very high wildfire risk.

Major incidents were declared in several areas including Suffolk , the Cairngorms , Hampshire and Holme Fen in Cambridgeshire, while firefighters faced what MPs described as increasingly demanding conditions.

At one stage in August, fire chiefs admitted they were under " incredible pressure " with 11 major fires in 48 hours and several wildfires across many parts of the West Midlands, as well as in Hampshire and south Wales.

The whole street was on fire: Inside the West Midlands wildfires

How did some houses survive the Stourbridge fire while neighbours lost everything?

The committee said the 2026 season had exposed weaknesses in national resilience, including access to aerial firefighting resources, securing water supplies during major incidents and coordinating resources at a national level.

MPs said the current system for obtaining aerial firefighting support was "no longer fit for purpose" and called for a detailed implementation plan for a UK aerial firefighting capability ahead of next year's wildfire season.

The report also urged ministers to fund a national wildfire prevention campaign and said activities such as using disposable barbecues, lighting campfires and discarding cigarettes during periods of elevated fire risk should become "socially unacceptable".

MPs welcomed the government's temporary restrictions on disposable barbecue sales during this summer's heatwave but said action should have been taken sooner.

A disposable barbecue was blamed for a fire that destroyed four homes in Stoke-on-Trent in August , while another major blaze in Macclesfield, Cheshire , was also thought to have been caused by one.

The committee stopped short of backing any single approach to land management, instead calling for an evidence-based "toolbox" including measures such as grazing, cutting, peatland restoration and prescribed burning where appropriate.

It also said ministers should recognise the role played by land managers and local communities in responding to wildfires and the physical and emotional toll such incidents can have.

Alistair Carmichael, chair of the committee, told the BBC: "What we've seen as serious wildfires this year is going to be normal in years going forward."

"If we don't get serious, if we don't have a strategy, if we don't put money behind it, then that is going to keep happening.

"We can't force the government to start spending money, but if they find themselves in the situation that they were this year, again next year, they will not be able to say that nobody warned them."

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: "Improving wildfire preparedness is a major government priority."

They said ministers were holding a summit this week with fire and rescue leaders, land managers and other organisations, and pointed to a pilot scheme involving six teams of specialist firefighters that can be deployed to major wildfire incidents across the country.

articles.title: The disputed story of the 'creepy' undercover police officer
articles.summary: Andrew Coles denies claims he deceived a young woman into sex while infiltrating an activist group.
articles.body:
Andrew Coles sings in a church choir, is active in local Conservative politics and was once an undercover Metropolitan Police officer – a so-called "spy cop".

Jessica – not her real name – is an animal rights activist who says he deceived her into sleeping with him.

This is a story about sex and lies. But who is telling the truth?

Coles, 66, lives in a thatched cottage in the Cambridgeshire countryside with his wife and their greyhound.

He is the brother of broadcaster the Reverend Richard Coles.

But between 1990 and 1995, he served in the Metropolitan Police Service's (MPS) undercover Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), which infiltrated political and protest groups.

For the past decade, its activities have been probed by the Undercover Policing Inquiry (UCPI) .

"The MPS has accepted that Andrew Coles had a sexual relationship with Jessica," wrote the force's commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, "and is disappointed he did not tell the truth to the inquiry."

Coles is also accused of appearing to advise colleagues to have similar relationships.

He vehemently denies the claims against him, insisting he is the victim of a deceit.

"It's payback, pure and simple," he says.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Coles lists resilience, bravery and ruthlessness as the qualities needed in a good undercover police officer.

"I suppose so," he says. "Though I didn't behave very differently to my own personality."

Coles's current life is a far cry from his covert past when, he says, he sometimes had to break the law to gain trust and maintain his cover.

"I took drugs – cannabis. It was necessary – you had to be vouched for," he says.

"I was given a lemon squeezy bottle, allegedly full of acid, and squirted it over a butcher's shop window.

"I was also involved in a raid on a chicken farm when some chickens were stolen and damage was done to the property."

The SDS had already existed for more than 20 years when Coles, then a constable in the Met, received a tap on the shoulder.

Taking the name Andy Davey from a dead child, he began making connections with the Animal Liberation Front, an extremist direct-action group.

"The work was certainly not everyone's cup of tea, but I protected a part of society from some very dangerous people, and I think I did a good job," he says.

In 1991, Jessica met Davey for the first time.

She was a naïve 19-year-old, she recalls, living in a shared east London terrace and looking for adventure.

Jessica, now 54, remembers Davey as an awkward older man who drove a van, which endeared him to her close circle of like-minded activists.

"Late in the evenings he would come to the house and we struggled to get rid of him," she says.

"Then one night, without warning, he went to kiss me. I didn't have the confidence to get out of the situation and he became my first proper boyfriend."

But he was not 24 as Jessica had thought. He was 32, married and had children.

Nor was he a fellow hunt saboteur. He was secretly gathering intelligence as part of a criminal inquiry into the ALF after several members were convicted of arson and bombing offences.

"He groomed me," she says. "He would sleep in my single bed several times a week, and I didn't know who he really was.

"It's difficult to describe it as rape, but he knew that having sex with me would have been against my consent."

Coles has admitted sharing Jessica's bed on one occasion but says there was never any sexual contact.

"Her story is not true, absolutely not true," he insists. When pressed about the weight of evidence, he concedes: "It is very hard to defeat."

That evidence includes two handwritten letters that Jessica, then staying in France, wrote to her best friend in 1993.

In the first, she writes: "It's really weird, but I'm still going out with Andy."

And in the second: "[Andy] suggested that we see other people because if I decided to stay here for another year... he wouldn't be getting enough sex."

Coles has a theory about the provenance of these letters.

"So, the first could have been written at the time. The second, what it talks about is absolute nonsense. I think it was written much later and added to the evidence bundle," he says.

"The handwriting is nothing like her handwriting in the original letter, which is almost a childlike scrawl. The second one is an elegant, joined-up cursive."

Jessica has shown the BBC more letters from the same period, written in noticeably different hands.

"If I write slowly, I can make it neat, but if I'm writing in a hurry or I'm angry, it's completely different," she says.

"The letters themselves are really embarrassing, and if I was to make something up it wouldn't have all that excruciatingly awful stuff in it."

Forensic graphologist Kate Barr told the BBC Jessica's handwriting "appeared to vary" and it was possible she had written both letters at around the same time.

Launched by Theresa May in 2015, the UCPI is examining claims officers deceived women into sexual relationships, spied on the family of the murdered teenager Stephen Lawrence, took the names of dead children and infiltrated groups without justification.

Giving evidence in 2024, Coles was quizzed about references in his intelligence reports to the "good looks" of female activists.

"Was the sexual attractiveness of the women you were mixing with on your mind?" he was asked.

"No, not for me," Coles replied, "but it was certainly a matter of... note".

Coles was then questioned about the accounts of various witnesses, many of whom did not know Jessica, who described him as a "sex pest", a "creep" and a "lech".

Some alleged he pursued women and sought unwanted sexual encounters.

Three people reported seeing him behaving intimately with Jessica in his van or emerging from her bedroom in only his boxer shorts.

Coles says their stories are "completely made-up".

"It's hardly surprising they'd want to get their own back on me," he adds.

Coles was unexpectedly exposed by his famous brother, who wrote in his 2014 autobiography: "My older brother Andy brought his own drama with him.

"He had joined Special Branch and was undercover, living a double life, infiltrated into some sinister organisation while his wife and baby daughter made do with unpredictable visits."

Coles was confirmed to be Andy Davey, or operative HN2, at the UCPI in 2018.

Does he regret his brother writing those words?

"It would have been easier had he not, but I hold no ill will; he's my brother and I love him deeply, so it is not an issue for me," Coles says.

The revelation was harder for Jessica, then in the process of setting up a business and art studio.

"My whole world came to a crashing halt," she says.

"They created this person, and they deployed him into my life, and my bed. It's a massive violation. It was like being raped by the state.

"He was spying on my parents, my friends. And for what? I was a hunt saboteur. I don't have a criminal record... and all these officers were just looking at people for rescuing chickens."

After leaving the Met in 2012, Coles served on Peterborough City Council and as deputy police and crime commissioner for Cambridgeshire.

But after his unmasking, the backlash was relentless.

Jessica and her supporters mounted a campaign against him, labelling him an abuser of women and protesting at council meetings.

Coles says: "They met with the leader of the council; they've written to charities I'm involved with, saying 'Do not trust this man'; they've produced leaflets.

"It's exhausting and there is always the threat of more violence."

Coles, a former president of Peterborough Conservative Association, lost his council seat in 2024 and has twice stood unsuccessfully for re-election.

Jessica says: "He should not be in a position of power. He was in a position of power when I had a relationship with him, and he abused that power in the worst possible way."

"No, it's because people need to know, and I don't want him to do it to anyone else."

In 2019 Coles confronted Jessica on a Peterborough housing estate.

"I turned around and he was about 10ft away from me and my colleague with his camera in my face, filming us and saying, 'You're going to jail,'" she says.

"It's the closest he'd been to me for 30 years and I just wanted to get away."

Coles admits he "snatched a few leaflets" out of a person's hand.

"My concern was they were distributing material to influence the outcome of the election," he says.

"They then made an allegation of theft and injury, and I was investigated by the police at the time, but nothing came of it."

In 2017, the Met investigated Coles's alleged relationship with Jessica.

No criminal charges were brought but he was told he would have faced a gross misconduct hearing had he not already left the force.

The campaign group Police Spies Out of Lives says undercover officers deceived more than 60 women into sexual relationships.

Jessica and eight other women have received formal apologies and a share of millions of pounds in compensation.

Some of those officers were informed by a special guidebook, the Tradecraft Manual, authored by Coles in 1995.

Under the heading 'Sexual Liaisons' he wrote: "If you have no other option but to become involved with a weary [a term he used for activists], you should try to have fleeting, disastrous relationships."

Was Coles encouraging officers to have sex with the people they were spying on?

"No, I was talking about relationships; if someone takes an interest in you and it becomes more than just a friendship, you can do something to break it," he says.

Yet the section is headed "Sexual Liaisons".

"I know, and it surprised me when I saw that because I don't think I wrote it," he adds.

Nonetheless, officers advised by Coles later had long-running sexual relationships with activists. Does he feel partly responsible?

"If I was responsible for their management, then absolutely, but I was only training them in the concepts," he says.

Jessica, who now lives in the south of England and fosters guinea pigs when not campaigning, says she will always be affected by her relationship with Coles.

"I feel like it's an attack on my honesty. I have to keep fighting. You know we all do, because it shouldn't happen to anyone else."

Does Jessica ever enter Coles's thoughts?

"I don't think of her. That's my deep and distant past. It has no relevance today," he says.

The UCPI is years behind schedule and still has no end date.

Next year, its outgoing chair, Sir John Mitting, is expected to rule on whether Coles or Jessica is telling the truth.

If you've been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at the BBC Action Line .

articles.title: Nuneaton farmer lost out by minutes in race for wildlife funding
articles.summary: Richard Peace is among thousands of farmers who missed out as funding was snapped up in hours.
articles.body:
The barn owls have become one of Richard Peace's favourite sights on the farm.

As dusk falls near the woods edging his land outside Nuneaton in Warwickshire, the birds emerge to hunt over fields he has spent years managing.

This year he wanted to do more to help them thrive.

To encourage the owls, Richard planned to leave some crops unharvested near the woodland where they live.

"Obviously that will bring some of the wildlife out of the woods, like voles and mice, and I was hoping that the barn owls would then thrive even more than they are already," he said.

But leaving part of a crop in the ground comes at a cost.

The government offers support to farmers carrying out environmental work through schemes that pay for so-called public goods, from improving habitats to boosting biodiversity.

For Richard, accessing some of that £310m funding seemed straightforward enough. All he had to do was submit an application.

What he did not realise was that he was entering a race against thousands of other farmers for that limited pot of cash.

"We looked at 8am and it wasn't live. I had things to do so I went to work on the farm," he said.

"Checked again at lunchtime, it was live and I started. We had a few errors but I did get to the end of the form and submitted it.

"I was minutes too late and the scheme had been subscribed. The money pot was exhausted."

Richard is among thousands of farmers who missed out after funding was snapped up within hours.

He believes smaller family farms may have been at a disadvantage.

While some larger businesses could dedicate staff to monitoring the application process, Richard spent the morning carrying out day-to-day work on the farm before returning to complete his submission.

The National Farmers' Union (NFU) had already warned that demand could outstrip the available funding.

Helen Fisher, who farms near Atherstone and is deputy regional chair of the NFU Midlands, said: "The scheme opened and closed in six hours. Nobody had anticipated that level of demand.

"We had been warning Defra there would be high demand and 12,000 farmers just couldn't get their applications in in time."

Richard believes a first-come, first-served system is the wrong way to allocate support.

"It should be available to everybody, those applications should then be evaluated," he said.

"If the scheme is oversubscribed the larger payments should be scaled back so that smaller farmers can get a slice of the larger pot."

Farmers in the Midlands often operate on a smaller scale than elsewhere in England, although regional data showing who ultimately benefited from the scheme is not publicly available.

Stories like Richard's have become increasingly familiar, and ministers have acknowledged concerns about the way applications were handled.

Farming Minister Stephen Morgan said: "I know some farmers who wanted to join SFI26 will be deeply disappointed not to have secured an agreement during Window 2, particularly given the challenges the sector has faced this year.

"I have heard those concerns and am determined to work closely with farmers as we learn lessons from this year and shape SFI27, including exploring alternatives to a first-come, first-served application process."

For Richard, the hope is that by next year the system will be fairer and allow more farmers to access support for projects that benefit wildlife.

If that happens, the barn owls he enjoys watching over his farm may have an even better chance of thriving.

articles.title: Far from fringe: How Israel’s mainstream parties vote with the far right
articles.summary: Al Jazeera analysed how every party in the Knesset voted on the most consequential measures affecting Palestinians.
articles.body:
Israelis head to the polls on October 27 in the first election since the genocide in Gaza and the wars on Lebanon and Iran, a vote widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rule.

Since the start of the war on Gaza in October 2023, Israel’s parliament, known as the Knesset, has passed or advanced a wave of laws and motions affecting Palestinians, from rejecting their statehood and backing annexation of the occupied West Bank to cutting off the aid they receive.

Israel’s Jewish-led opposition casts itself as the alternative to Netanyahu’s right-wing government, but when it comes to Palestinians, the two often vote as one .

Left and right are the most common way of mapping where parties stand on a political spectrum. The left generally favours more state spending and is more liberal on immigration and minority rights. The right generally favours lower taxes, tighter borders and a cohesive national identity.

In Israel, the labels work differently. They are defined less by economics than by the conflict with Palestinians. Broadly, the left has been associated with territorial compromise and negotiations, and the right with opposing a Palestinian state and supporting the growth of illegal settlements.

Israel’s political spectrum as a whole has shifted right, with once-fringe positions on Palestinians now very much the mainstream view. According to Palestinian political analyst Ehab Jabareen , much of Jewish Israeli politics now works from “assumptions that would have been treated as right-wing a generation ago”.

The chart below shows generally where each party sits on that spectrum today.

Israel’s parties and coalitions, explained

No party has ever won an outright majority in Israel’s Knesset.

To govern, a prime minister needs at least 61 of its 120 seats, which means building a coalition of smaller parties, often with competing demands. That gives small parties outsized leverage: if one walks out, the government can fall.

After the November 2022 election, Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud, the largest party with 32 seats, formed a 64-seat coalition. Its partners were two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, and the far-right Religious Zionism alliance, a joint list of the Religious Zionism and Otzma Yehudit parties. It was Israel’s most right-wing government to date.

The far-right leaders are among the most powerful figures in government. Bezalel Smotrich, head of Religious Zionism, is finance minister and also holds authority over civilian affairs in the occupied West Bank, including settlement planning.

Itamar Ben-Gvir, head of Otzma Yehudit, is national security minister, in charge of the police. He and Smotrich have both pushed for annexation and settlement expansion, and both have used the threat of quitting to shape government policy.

The coalition has shifted repeatedly since. Benny Gantz’s National Unity alliance joined after the October 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas and left in June 2024, and Gideon Sa’ar’s New Hope joined that September. Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit quit over a “ceasefire” in Gaza in January 2025 and returned two months later. In July 2025, United Torah Judaism (UTJ) walked out over a stalled bill to exempt ultra-Orthodox men from military service. Shas, another party representing ultra-Orthodox voters, withdrew its ministers at the same time, but stayed in the coalition.

When parliament dissolved in July ahead of the October 27 election, the coalition held 60 seats: Likud (32), Shas (11), Otzma Yehudit (7), Religious Zionism (6) and New Hope (4).

Opposition in Israel does not mean left. Yesh Atid, led by Yair Lapid, was the largest party in the outgoing Knesset, with 24 seats. Benny Gantz’s Blue and White was second. Both are centrist and have campaigned against a judicial overhaul proposed by Netanyahu and his coalition of religious and nationalist partners.

Yisrael Beiteinu, led by Avigdor Lieberman, is secular and right wing. Lieberman is a former Netanyahu ally who opposes draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men.

Labor, now part of the Democrats, is the only Jewish party in the outgoing Knesset that openly backs a two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict.

The Arab-led parties, which represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, differ in ideology but share opposition to the occupation. Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, made history in 2021 as the first Arab party to enter an Israeli government. Hadash-Ta’al, led by Ayman Odeh and Ahmad Tibi, has never joined one. It is running in this election as part of the Joint List, alongside Balad.

Al Jazeera analysed the 10 most consequential Knesset votes affecting Palestinians between July 2024 and March 2026.

In Israel, a bill must pass three votes in the Knesset to become law. Most votes need only a simple majority of members present, and parties often stay away on purpose, either to deny a bill legitimacy or to avoid going on record. As a result, some votes in this analysis involve only a fraction of the 120-seat parliament. Some bills passed by wide margins, while others scraped through by a handful of votes.

What the data shows is that the left barely exists. The only consistent opposition came from the Arab-led parties and the four-seat Democrats, which together held 14 of the 120 seats in the last Knesset.

The results are shown in the graphic below, with a summary of the key votes beneath it.

In February 2024, the Knesset backed a cabinet statement against unilateral recognition of a Palestinian state by 99 votes to 11.

The coalition, Yisrael Beiteinu and most members of Yesh Atid and National Unity – led by Gantz and comprising members of his Blue and White and Sa’ar’s New Hope party – voted in favour. Labor boycotted the vote, while only the Arab-led parties voted against.

The pattern repeated five months later. In July 2024, a resolution calling a Palestinian state an “existential danger” passed 68 to nine. National Unity, which by then had lost Sa’ar’s New Hope faction, joined the coalition and Yisrael Beiteinu in favour, Yesh Atid and Labor stayed away, and again only the Arab-led parties voted against.

Ahead of the election, the Jerusalem News Syndicate asked Israeli politicians from across the political spectrum, “Does your party support the establishment of a Palestinian state?” Every politician featured said “no”.

The Knesset’s votes reflect the public that elects it. Israelis’ view of Palestinian statehood had been declining for a decade, and it hardened sharply after October 7.

In spring 2023, 35 percent of Israelis told the Pew Research Center that Israel and a Palestinian state could coexist peacefully, down from 50 percent in 2013. By 2024, months after the attack, that had fallen to 26 percent. It reached 21 percent in 2025 and 17 percent in 2026, the first time a majority of Israelis have explicitly said coexistence is impossible.

In July 2025, a nonbinding declaration calling for the annexation of the occupied West Bank, including the Jordan Valley, passed 71 to 13. Yesh Atid and National Unity boycotted it. Labor joined the Arab-led parties in voting against the measure.

When annexation came to an actual bill, the lines blurred further. On October 22, 2025, during a United States vice-presidential visit, a bill that would apply Israeli law to the occupied West Bank passed in a preliminary reading by a single vote, 25 to 24:

For: Religious Zionism, Otzma Yehudit and Yisrael Beiteinu

Against: Yesh Atid, Labor and the Arab-led parties

Likud officially opposed the bill, with only lawmaker Yuli Edelstein voting for it. Had UTJ’s four votes in favour gone the other way, the bill would have failed.

The ban on UNRWA , the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees, drew the widest support of any binding law in the analysis.

Set up by the UN General Assembly in 1949 after the Nakba – or “catastrophe”, an Arabic word referring to the ethnic cleansing of Palestine in 1948 – UNRWA provides schools, healthcare, food aid and other basic services to nearly six million registered Palestinian refugees in Gaza, the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria.

In October 2024, the first of two bills barring the agency from operating in territory Israel considers sovereign, including occupied East Jerusalem, passed 92 to 10. The second, cutting off all state contact with UNRWA, passed 87 to nine. Both laws took effect in January 2025, despite warnings from the UN and Western governments that they would cripple aid operations.

Netanyahu’s ruling coalition, Yisrael Beiteinu, Yesh Atid and National Unity all voted in favour, as did the Labor members of parliament who were present. The Arab-led parties were the only ones to vote against.

The election may change who governs Israel, but not necessarily how its parliament votes on Palestinians, especially as the electorate itself moves further right.

articles.title: Pakistan arrests man hunted by US over $126m postage fraud case
articles.summary: Faheem Akram allegedly sold more than 5 million fake postage labels for a fixed price of $2 a piece.
articles.body:
Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.

Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.

He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.

Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.

According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.

US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.

The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.

An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.

Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.

If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

articles.title: Surging fuel prices push UK inflation rate to 3.5% ahead of Budget
articles.summary: Inflation accelerated to 3.5% from 3.1% in the year to September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
articles.body:
The pace of UK price rises accelerated ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices.

The rate of inflation rose to 3.5% from 3.1% in the year to September, its quickest pace since October 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle has soared in recent months as conflicts in the Middle East and Europe continue to squeeze global oil supplies.

The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly £25bn in September, adding to pressure on Healey as he gears up for the Budget.

Petrol prices in September were the highest since August 2022, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p per litre to 169.5p per litre between August and September, while diesel rose to 192.5p per litre.

Motor fuel prices overall rose by 29.8% in the period covered by the figures.

ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said September's "notable" increase meant inflation was at its highest rate in almost a year.

The wars in the middle east and Ukraine have pushed up fuel prices. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran after US and Israeli attacks has severely disrupted a major global supply line for crude oil, while oil refining capacity has been hampered globally by Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's infrastructure.

As well as fuel prices, the increase was driven by rising prices for airfares, computer games and live events, Fitzner said.

With a week to go until he delivers the Budget, Healey said: "We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide."

He said the International Monetary Fund last week had praised the UK government for its "fiscal discipline", and that the government has just given the go-ahead for getting more gas from the North Sea's Jackdaw field .

The Budget on 28 October will "keep up this momentum", he said, by sticking to the government's self-imposed fiscal rules, and by driving "growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space".

But the figures came as the ONS said the government borrowed £25bn in September, £1.8bn higher than a year earlier, as higher inflation helped to push up debt interest costs.

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the borrowing figures "painted a dismal picture" ahead of Healey's Budget. She said the amount borrowed in September was higher than analyst expectations as well as spending watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)'s forecast.

"This reinforces our view that the Chancellor will deliver a cautious Budget on 28th October that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal choices for next year," she said.

articles.title: Australian lawmaker has both legs amputated after allegedly deliberate attack by car rammer
articles.summary: The Australian lawmaker hit by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has now had both legs amputated, her husband announced Wednesday.
articles.body: The Australian lawmaker hit by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has now had both legs amputated, her husband announced Wednesday. Helen Haines, an independent federal MP, remains in a critical condition in hospital after Monday’s incident, which unfolded mid-afternoon on a main road outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, northeastern Victoria. “Helen’s left leg was amputated on Monday. We had been hoping that her right leg would be saved, but… the surgeons had to also remove her right leg,” Phil Haines, the MP’s husband of nearly 40 years, told a press conference at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne. “But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable,” he added. A 43-year-old man, Brendan Nugent, faced court on Wednesday charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Speaking after Phil Haines at the same news conference, Governor-General Sam Mostyn said she was keeping King Charles III updated on developments. The governor-general is appointed by the king as Australia’s formal head of state, though the country is led by a prime minister under a parliamentary system. “Australia is still reeling with the shock and distress of this terrible attack,” Mostyn said. “I know that here in Victoria, in particular, people are simply dumbfounded and finding it very hard to fathom the scale of this tragedy.” As a pile of bouquets grew outside Haines’ electorate office, her husband urged people to consider donating instead. “She loves flowers, but it’s a bit difficult to look after many bunches of flowers,” Phil Haines said. “We will ask people if they would like to support Helen financially to make a donation to Save the Children Fund.” Security briefings Though police are still to determine if the incident was politically motivated, the alleged attack shocked the country and has shone a spotlight on the safety of its political leaders. Members of parliament received in-depth security briefings in Canberra on Wednesday as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) commissioner pointed to rising reports of harassment and threats against federal parliamentarians. Commissioner Krissy Barrett told a news conference that authorities were seeing “increasing political polarization and anti-government sentiment, conspiracy-driven and grievance-based behaviors.” “Lone actors motivated by a convergence of personal grievance, mental health vulnerabilities, and ideological concerns,” were contributing to the rising trend, she added. Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush said police had no intelligence on Haines’ alleged attacker that pointed to an imminent risk. In a very short court hearing on Wednesday morning, Nugent’s lawyer said Nugent had a rare neurological condition – and was currently unmedicated. No application for bail was made, and the next hearing is scheduled for February 4.
