articles.title: Who owns India’s textile traditions in age of AI-enabled mass production?
articles.summary: Technological tools meant to preserve a craft are now able to digitally reproduce it without involving the craftsperson.
articles.body:
Bitupan Deka was out shopping for a “gamusa” (traditional scarf) with his mother in India’s northeastern state of Meghalaya when he noticed something unusual.

“Every shop selling the scarf had the same handful of patterns repeated over and over,” he told Al Jazeera over the telephone from Shillong, the capital of Meghalaya.

“When I asked around, I found that weavers in Sualkuchi [district in neighbouring Assam state] are paid a one-time fee of roughly 2,000 rupees [$21] for each design they develop, instead of royalties. Cutting down the number of designs they produce was a cost-saving practice followed by the manufacturers.”

This discovery prompted Deka, an assistant professor of computer technology at Shillong’s MIT University, to create a system that can produce infinite new designs for such fabrics.

“My work isn’t meant to replace the traditional designers. I hope, instead, that it will become a tool in their hands to create new and modern motifs more easily, so the consumers can have variety,” Deka said.

Once the patent, which is being applied for under the research and development department of his university, comes through, Deka plans to monetise the system by making it a commercial designing service that the textile industry can avail.

In India’s varied textile traditions, patterns and motifs carry the memory of a place and the mythology of its people – sometimes even the history of migrations.

The designs are imagined by weavers from things that exist around them, and then painted with locally available colours, mostly using carved clay and wooden frames. These weavers do not simply reproduce a pattern; they inherit it. Their hands hesitate where their grandmother’s did, and they know why a particular flower must face left.

A computer has no such inheritance or hesitation. It learns by analysing pictures and repeating them in endless variations. And yet, as Deka’s system shows, the computer can now draw and weave the same flower.

The Rekh Sanganeri Dataset is a similar system developed for hand-block printed Sanganeri textiles from the western Indian state of Rajasthan. It includes high-resolution images of printed patterns, annotated down to ink bleed and slight misalignment – the imperfections that are the hallmark of the handmade work.

Its developer, Reddy Sai Nivas C, says it should be used as a resource for research and art, not as a substitute for artisans.

But the disclaimer is the paradox: Tools built to preserve a craft are making its visual language easier to digitally reproduce without involving the craftsperson.

Dinesh Chhipa comes from one of the oldest Chhipa families, an artisan and merchant caste renowned for dyeing and block printing. He is a Bagru designer – a block printing technique from Bagru town in the western state of Rajasthan – and a textile businessman.

“Traditional craft is slow to produce. Even if someone offered us a fortune, we wouldn’t be able to produce these pieces in mass numbers, so I don’t fault those using digital technology and AI to fill the gap,” he told Al Jazeera.

“But don’t borrow craft and regional names like Bagru and Jaipuri [named after the capital city of Rajasthan]. These designs and motifs were born out of a culture and necessities of the communities they come from.”

Who owns culture when it turns into plain data?

India has been digitising its textile memory for years – from the Botanical Survey of India’s historical collections to the Bharatiya Vastra Shilpa Kosh, a national portal built by the state-run National Institute of Fashion Technology and the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC).

Without documentation, the fragile traditions and knowledge could disappear. But digitisation also allows the same archive to be used by an AI system seeking to reproduce these crafts at scale.

At the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February this year, Indian software company Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) showcased Bridgital Loom, an AI system that converts textile designs into loom-ready instructions. LED lights on the loom guide a weaver through the thread sequences of intricate Banarasi and Kanchipuram patterns – named after the cities where these iconic arts grew.

TCS says the technology helps weavers execute complex designs faster and with fewer errors, and is meant to be a bridge between the artisans and technology. A pilot project that uses the loom is already under way at Kanchipuram, a town in southern Tamil Nadu state.

In an interview with the online platform Digit at the New Delhi summit, the head of AI strategy at Bridgital Loom, Muthulakshmi Nellaiappan, pointed out that a new weaver takes more than 15 years to master the art.

“With the technologies we have in hand … the younger weaver who has just entered the skill can become a master much sooner,” she said.

Technology flattens the master-apprentice hierarchy of traditional knowledge systems. The weaver no longer has to conceptualise or remember patterns, colours and codes; he blindly follows the machine’s instructions, handing creativity and memory to AI.

Nellaiappan said that since a large percentage of India’s looms are non-electronic, TCS has ensured its system works with handlooms as well and that it was essential for scaling up the technology.

But digital looms also raise another question: Who owns culture when it turns into plain data?

For generations, India’s textile knowledge sat outside intellectual property systems. It lived in community memory, passed from master to apprentice with no certificate of ownership. Kanchipuram, Mekhela-Sador, Sanganeri and Banarasi are names for places that these textiles helped shape, not merely emerged from.

Now, this knowledge is entering generative models that owe nothing to these traditions.

For designers and manufacturers, the possibilities are seductive: Motifs combined at will, colours changed with a command, and thousands of designs generated instantly. The machine offers abundance.

The artisan, on the other hand, has always lived with scarcity: Of money, bargaining power, or recognition.

Ananthalakshmi Vadivel, a third-generation weaver and owner of Vadivel Silk Looms in Kanchipuram, says their venture is already competing in the market with cheaper Kanchipuram sarees produced on electronic looms.

“Perhaps, with AI, these sellers can create trending designs faster and cheaper to attract mass consumers. But these imitations can never replace the original,” she told Al Jazeera.

“There will always be a market for authentic Kanchipuram and handcrafted textiles, no matter how much technology makes the imitation cheaper. True Kanchipuram weave, colour, and designs can only be created by hand, and discerning buyers know this.”

Then again, the question is no longer whether AI can recreate a textile. It sure can. The question is: Who gets paid when it does?

In December 2025, the federal government’s Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade floated a statutory “blanket licence” – a system where AI developers could train models on lawfully obtained copyrighted material without seeking permission from each rights holder. Once commercialised, those systems would owe royalties to copyright owners at rates set by the government.

But intellectual property (IP) laws assume a traceable work with a traceable author. A motif, on the other hand, is communal property, its technique passed down through generations with no single originator.

In such cases, who is entitled to royalty and copyright? The artisan who first created the design? The photographer who documented it? The researcher who assembled the dataset? The developer who built the tool? India’s laws offer no clear answers. The artisan whose name never appeared on a label may once again be missing from the paperwork.

Meanwhile, the government is planning a dedicated AI-handloom research department under the Centre of Excellence for Handloom Technology at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) in the capital, New Delhi. Inaugurated in August, the $1.4m facility aims to modernise India’s handloom sector by combining traditional weaving heritage with contemporary technology.

The government also plans to register thousands of weavers and fit their handlooms with sensors that convert weave patterns into digital data, and issue QR-coded tags to trace provenance. Maharashtra’s Vingatha system does something similar at the state level by authenticating handloom sarees such as Paithani and Karvat Kathi.

The idea is simple: If a saree can tell you where it came from, the person who made it becomes harder to erase.

While these measures cannot stop AI-enabled design and mass production, they may give artisans more visibility and turn each piece into an archive.

In art galleries, the traditional textiles are increasingly shedding the label of craft for the more lucrative category of contemporary art.

Gurjeet Singh, an artist from Chandigarh city, recently hosted a textile-based solo show in New York. His work transforms discarded fabrics, buttons and embroidered scraps into sculptures that explore queer identity and social prejudices surrounding gender and sexuality.

Sayan Chanda, an Indian artist based in London, works with cut and rewoven vintage Bengali quilts to question fixed notions of cultural belonging. Gurugram-based artist Sumakshi Singh uses delicate embroidery and suspended thread structures to reconstruct the architectural fragments of vanished homes, gardens and personal histories. There are many more.

In New Delhi, 20 such artisans and craft-led collectives featured last month at an art show celebrating the traditional textile crafts.

“Our aim is to present these traditional crafts as living practices that continue to evolve through contemporary artisans, rather than as heritage to be archived. Kanmai Payun, one of the artists featured in the show, for example, is the last practitioner of Fulor Saneki, a flower pattern used by Assamese weavers. We encouraged her to teach her 17-year-old son so the craft outlives her,” Aparupa Ray Ganguly, the curator of the show, told Al Jazeera.

But as textiles gain value in art galleries, their makers do not necessarily gain automatic control over their work.

In April, another art exhibition in New Delhi, titled No ‘One’ Maker, saw artisans missing from the show’s preview, exposing how traditional textiles are aestheticised, but the people who carry that knowledge remain unrecognised.

“You cannot separate the names from the community. Call your mass-produced work digital prints and leave the traditional names to the original artisans,” says Chhipa, the artisan and merchant from Rajasthan.

articles.title: Alabama governor commutes death sentence as doubts emerge about evidence in murder conviction
articles.summary: Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey commuted Toforest Johnson's death sentence, but his attorneys say the fight for a new trial and full exoneration continues.
articles.body: Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey, a Republican, commuted the sentence of a death row inmate on Tuesday after the current Jefferson County district attorney and several former judges and prosecutors raised concerns about his conviction. The governor said she was commuting Toforest Johnson’s death sentence to life in prison without parole. Johnson, who has long maintained his innocence, was convicted in the 1995 murder of Jefferson County Deputy Sheriff William Hardy. He remains incarcerated at the Holman Correctional Facility. "When presented with Mr. Johnson’s case, I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death," Ivey said in a statement. "My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole." Ivey has commuted the death sentences of three death row inmates since she became governor in 2017. She has also overseen 27 executions during her tenure, which will end in January because she is term-limited and cannot run for re-election. GOP GOV DEWINE URGES OHIO TO ABOLISH THE DEATH PENALTY, SAYS IT IS NO LONGER A DETERRENT The governor spared his life despite Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall urging her last week to reject the clemency request and "respect the jury's decision" and the rulings of the courts reviewing Johnson's case. On July 19, 1995, Hardy was shot twice in the head as he was working off-duty security outside a hotel in Birmingham. Johnson said he was on the other side of the city when the shooting happened. One of Johnson’s attorneys, Ty Alper, said he and his client are grateful to Ivey for "diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution," but added that they will continue to fight to overturn the conviction. "Toforest Johnson is innocent. Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family," Alper said in a statement. LAWYERS, EXPERTS URGE TENNESSEE GOVERNOR TO COMMUTE CHRISTA PIKE’S SENTENCE AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION Johnson's attorneys have waged a yearslong legal battle to secure a new trial. His push for a new trial has received national attention and attracted widespread support, including from prominent lawyers, such as the original prosecutor in his case, as well as celebrities such as Kim Kardashian. Several former judges and prosecutors have joined supporters seeking a new trial for Johnson over questions about his conviction. Former Alabama Attorney General Bill Baxley, former Chief Justices of the Alabama Supreme Court Sonny Hornsby and Drayton Nabers and other former judges and prosecutors have submitted briefs or written editorials backing a new trial. Jefferson County District Attorney Danny Carr, who was elected in 2018, is among those who have backed Johnson’s call for a new trial. In 2024, Carr wrote in a court filing that the "evidence in this case has unraveled over 20 years." Carr said that credible alibi witnesses place Johnson in another area at the time of the shooting. He also said there are multiple reasons to doubt the key prosecution witness, who "claimed she overheard Johnson confess to the murder on a three-way phone call on which she was eavesdropping." She received a $5,000 reward in 2001 for her assistance in the case. Johnson’s lawyers said that the state withheld evidence of monetary incentive for her testimony. articles.title: Venus Cazimi in Scorpio on October 23: 4 Zodiac Signs Could Finally See the Truth About Love and Money
articles.summary: For three weeks, Venus has been walking backwards through Scorpio, and the questions it raised have mostly stayed in the background.
articles.body: For three weeks, Venus has been walking backwards through Scorpio, and the questions it raised have mostly stayed in the background. On the night of October 23, they step into the light. As per Western astrology, Venus will reach its cazimi at 0°45′ Scorpio at 11:44 p.m. ET (8:50 p.m. PT), the exact moment it meets the Sun. For four signs in particular, that moment could bring clear answers about love, trust and money.What a Cazimi IsCazimi comes from an Arabic term meaning "in the heart." It describes a planet that sits within roughly 17 arcminutes of the Sun, close enough to be absorbed into its light. Planets near the Sun are usually seen as weakened. A planet at the exact centre is the opposite, and astrologers treat it as purified and strengthened.For Venus, this event also marks the midpoint of its retrograde. Venus turned retrograde on October 3 at 8°29′ Scorpio and will turn direct in mid-November at nearly 23° Libra. The cazimi sits right in between, where the old cycle ends and a new one begins.Why It Matters This YearThe timing stacks several turning points into a single weekend. The Sun enters Scorpio on October 23 at 5:37 a.m. ET. Venus meets it that night. Mercury turns retrograde at 20°59′ Scorpio about three and a half hours later. Venus then slips back into Libra in the early hours of October 25. All of this happens in the sign of intensity, secrets and shared resources, which is why the topics in play are trust, desire and money tied to other people.Venus rules attraction and value. Scorpio rules what is hidden. A Cazimi in Scorpio asks what the heart actually wants, once the polite answers are stripped away.Scorpio: The Honest Answer About What You WantScorpio hosts the Sun and Venus together, so this sign feels the event in person. A feeling that has been kept private since the summer may need a name. It could be a wish to leave a relationship, a need for more commitment, or a decision about a job that pays well but costs too much.Write the answer down before speaking. A clear sentence delivered calmly will land far better than a long confession. Scorpio's strength this weekend is certainty, and the best use of it is to set one boundary and keep it.Taurus: The Truth About Shared MoneyTaurus sits opposite Scorpio, and the Full Moon in Taurus arrives on October 26. Between the two events, shared finances come into focus. A joint account, a rent split or a family loan may show an imbalance that was easy to ignore before.The Cazimi favours a plain look at numbers. Print the last three statements, list who pays for what and note anything that does not match. Taurus tends to avoid conflict when money is involved, and this is the moment to speak up while the facts are fresh.Libra: A Relationship Question Reaches Its AnswerVenus rules Libra, and the planet moves back into Libra on October 25. The cazimi hands Libra a rare gift: a clear view of a partnership that has felt unsettled. A talk that kept stalling may finally move, because both sides are more honest than before.Libra often tries to keep every side happy. This week, the better path is to say which outcome feels fair and why. If a partner, friend or business contact wants a different result, a respectful conversation can still keep the bond intact. The goal is an agreement that both people can stand behind.Aquarius: Control and Closeness MeetPluto in Aquarius turned direct on October 15, and Venus formed a square to it on October 20. The cazimi lands in the middle of that story. For Aquarius, the theme is how much independence a relationship allows, and how much honesty it needs.A partner may ask for more openness, or a friend may ask where the limits are. Offer details, not slogans. Explain what space is needed and what commitment is on offer. Aquarius gets the best results by showing what can be counted on, not by describing what feels uncomfortable.What Everyone Else Should DoThe other eight signs will feel a milder version of the same pattern. Cancer, Virgo, Capricorn and Pisces can use the weekend to review budgets and sort old messages. Gemini should double-check emails and texts once Mercury turns retrograde. Aries, Leo and Sagittarius may feel impatient with slow replies and should save major decisions for after Venus turns direct.Avoid signing new joint contracts or making big purchases until mid-November. articles.title: “Never ask what I would do”: The advice Steve Jobs gave Tim Cook before leaving Apple
articles.summary: When Steve Jobs handed over the reins of Apple to Tim Cook, he left him with a piece of advice that Cook has never forgotten.
articles.body: When Steve Jobs handed over the reins of Apple to Tim Cook, he left him with a piece of advice that Cook has never forgotten. He told him not to spend time wondering what he would have done, but to focus on making the right decisions himself.“Never ask what I would do, just do the right thing,” Jobs told Cook.Cook recalled the conversation in an interview with CBS Sunday Morning, explaining how Jobs wanted him to lead Apple in his own way rather than feel pressured to follow the same path.Cook joined Apple in 1998 and took over as CEO in 2011, after Jobs stepped down because of his declining health. Jobs died in October that year, but his advice has continued to shape how Cook thinks about leadership.Why Steve Jobs didn't want Apple to look backJobs had a reason for giving Cook that advice. He had seen what could happen when a company became too focused on trying to recreate the vision of its founder.According to Fortune, Jobs had noticed this while observing Disney after the death of its founder, Walt Disney. Jobs knew the company well. He had bought Pixar from Lucasfilm in 1986, and Disney went on to acquire the animation studio in 2006.During that time, Jobs noticed that people at Disney were spending too much time discussing what Walt Disney would have done instead of making decisions for themselves.“He had watched Disney go through this paralysis of sitting around and talking about what Walt [Disney] would do. And he did not want that for Apple,” Cook explained.Jobs wanted to avoid the same situation at Apple. He knew the company would have to change and grow after his departure, and he didn't want his successor to feel that every decision had to match his own thinking.How Steve Jobs prepared Tim Cook to become CEOCook said Apple had never really experienced a normal change of leadership at the top. Previous transitions had happened during difficult periods, and Jobs wanted his own departure to be different.He eventually invited Cook to his home and offered him the CEO position. But along with the offer, he made one thing clear: Cook didn't have to lead the way he did.Looking back, Cook said that advice took a huge weight off his shoulders.“I’ll never forget that and it was such a gift for me, because he took off of my shoulder this question of, ‘What would Steve do?’” Cook said.Instead of constantly comparing himself with Jobs, Cook decided to concentrate on being the best leader he could be.“I just put my head down and thought, ‘I’m going to be the best version of myself,’” he recalled.Cook had joined Apple less than a year after Jobs returned to the company as interim CEO. He became chief operating officer in 2005 before taking over as CEO six years later.Since then, Cook has spent years building on Apple's existing strengths while putting his own stamp on the company.The leadership lessons Cook learned from JobsCook says some of Apple's core principles have stayed with him over the years. These include teamwork, open debate, focus and a high standard for the products the company makes.Jobs believed that people could achieve more by sharing ideas and challenging each other's thinking than by working in isolation.“He had the vision that the collaboration was something that would produce great results. That one plus one is equal to three, not two,” Cook said.He also recalled Jobs' belief that a good idea could become even better when people were willing to discuss it honestly. Sometimes, that meant calling a colleague late at night because a new idea couldn't wait until the next morning.But teamwork was only one part of Jobs' approach. He also believed that knowing what to ignore was just as important as knowing what to pursue.“[Jobs] had an idea of focus that you say ‘no’ to a thousand things to say ‘yes’ to the one that’s truly important,” Cook said.Jobs expected a lot from the people around him. For him, doing a job well wasn't always enough. He wanted people to push themselves to produce something exceptional.That approach became a familiar part of Apple's culture, from the way its teams worked to the attention paid to its products.Steve Jobs also gave advice to other business leadersCook wasn't the only business leader who turned to Jobs for guidance. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz have also spoken about advice they received from the Apple co-founder.Benioff recalled in a 2024 episode of Lenny's Podcast that Jobs helped him work through what he described as “entrepreneurs block”.Jobs challenged him to think bigger, including growing Salesforce's business tenfold within two years, winning a major customer for its automation product and building an application economy.Benioff took that advice as a push to create an app marketplace. The result was AppExchange, Salesforce's platform for business applications. He later credited Jobs' guidance with influencing his career and gave Apple the App Store trademark and the appstore.com domain.Schultz also sought Jobs' advice during a difficult period for Starbucks in 2008. After hearing about the company's problems, Jobs suggested replacing the entire leadership team. His reasoning was straightforward: if the existing executives weren't right for the company's future, many would eventually leave anyway.Schultz initially struggled with the idea but later said Jobs had been right. All but one member of the leadership team eventually departed.For Cook, though, Jobs' advice was about something more personal. He wasn't expected to become another Steve Jobs. He was expected to make his own decisions and take responsibility for them.And that may be the most lasting lesson Jobs left him with: respecting a founder's legacy doesn't mean trying to be that person. Sometimes, the best way to carry a company forward is to find your own way of leading it.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: U.K. approves long-delayed gas field in the North Sea despite climate concerns
articles.summary: Britain on Wednesday approved the Jackdaw North Sea gas field, ending years of legal and political wrangling that had pitted the Labour government’s climate commitments against its push to bolster energy security.
articles.body: Britain on Wednesday approved the Jackdaw North Sea gas field, ending years of legal and political wrangling that had pitted the Labour government’s climate commitments against its push to bolster energy security. Britain’s energy minister, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said the project will start to supply gas to British homes and businesses from as early as the end of this month. At the same time, she said a new Energy Wealth Fund would be established by the government with a £2 billion downpayment to reinvest oil and gas revenues into the climate transition. Fahnbulleh said Jackdaw was expected to increase domestic gas production by around 6% at its peak and support the country’s gas supply over its lifespan of up to 11 years, boosting energy security and protecting hundreds of jobs. “At a time when people are really struggling, it’s right that we look in a responsible way at maximizing the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” said Prime Minister Andy Burnham. “Even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.” Adura, the joint venture between energy giants Shell SHEL.L and Norway’s Equinor that operates the project, has said Jackdaw will produce up to 40,000 barrels of oil equivalent of natural gas per day at peak output. The fate of Jackdaw had been in limbo for years. The previous Conservative government approved the project in 2022, but climate activists challenged the decision in court alongside approval for the Rosebank oil and gas field. A 2025 ruling barred operators from extracting oil or gas until they received fresh government consent that takes into account emissions from the burning of the fields’ hydrocarbons. The decision has taken on added significance for Burnham since he took office in July. Britain’s high energy costs for households and industry have weighed on the economy, while President Donald Trump has repeatedly urged Burnham to expand drilling in the North Sea to help lower prices. At the same time, the issue has become a rallying point for climate activists, who say approving new fossil fuel projects undermines Labour’s green pledges and ignores warnings from a summer of record-breaking heat across Europe.

articles.title: One man collected it all: Inside Hyderabad’s Salar Jung Museum, one of India’s largest single-collector museums, including the Veiled Rebecca and mysterious musical clock
articles.summary: Imagine an art collection so precious and so rare that a museum can be built around it.
articles.body: Imagine an art collection so precious and so rare that a museum can be built around it. Well, it happened with the massive art collection of Nawab Mir Yousuf Ali Khan, popularly known as Salar Jung III. Three generations of the Salar Jung family were known for their passion for collecting art and literature. After Salar Jung III died in 1949, his art collection was left without an inheritor. The late Nawab’s family decided to present this treasure to the nation, and thus, the government established a museum around the collection. The museum opened to the public in 1951, and the Salar Jung Museum Act was passed in 1961, declaring it an ‘Institution of National Importance’ by the Government of India.Located on the southern bank of the Musi River and close to the Charminar, the museum offers an unexpected way to explore Hyderabad. Beyond the famous Hyderabadi biryani, dense bazaars and historic monuments lies a world assembled by a man who seemingly couldn't resist bringing a fascinating object home.The man behind the mountain of treasuresThe museum was established in 1951, but the art was collected over decades and came from around the world. After stepping down from the post of Dewan (Prime Minister), Salar Jung III dedicated his life to building a collection of art from around the world. Dewan Deodi, the ancestral residence of the Salar Jung family, was visited by merchants and travellers from all corners of the world, who brought works of art to his attention and offered them for sale.Before him, his family members were also nobles who served as important ministers under the Nizams of Hyderabad. While Salar Jung I (Mir Turab Ali Khan) modernised Hyderabad’s infrastructure and education, Salar Jung III (Mir Yousuf Ali Khan) gathered much of the art we see in the museum today. He was responsible for creating one of the world’s largest private collections.His own travels were also added to the collection. European paintings, Persian carpets, Chinese porcelain, Japanese art, Indian sculptures and exquisite decorative objects eventually found their way into his orbit. The museum, containing a lifetime’s collection, opened to the public on December 16, 1951, and Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister, inaugurated it. It moved to its present building in 1968, which Dr Zakir Husain, President of India, inaugurated.Today, the museum's official collection figures include more than 46,000 art objects, over 8,000 manuscripts and upwards of 60,000 printed books, spread across galleries devoted to Indian, European, Middle Eastern and Far Eastern art. In other words, you could visit the famous highlights and still leave feeling that you have only scratched the surface.Veiled Rebecca: Marble that plays tricks on your eyesIf there is one artwork that deserves a moment of undivided attention, it is the celebrated Veiled Rebecca.At first glance, the sculpture looks like a woman draped in a delicate, almost transparent veil. Look closer, and the real wonder becomes apparent: the veil, its folds and the figure beneath it have all been carved from a single block of marble. The stone seems impossibly soft, as though the artist could have lifted the fabric away with a gentle tug.Created in 1863 by Italian sculptor Giovanni Maria Benzoni, the work depicts Rebecca, a biblical figure. Salar Jung I acquired it during a visit to Italy in 1876. It is one of the museum's prized masterpieces and a striking example of 19th-century Neoclassical sculpture.The cleverness lies in the details: the delicate creases, the fall of the fabric and the way light moves across the marble. You know it is solid stone, yet your eyes insist on seeing cloth. It is the sort of artwork that makes you wonder how much patience, skill and sheer confidence it takes to carve something so fragile-looking out of such an unforgiving material.The musical clock that steals the showThen comes the museum's most entertaining exercise in patience: the musical clock.In the clock gallery, visitors gather around a remarkable 19th-century timepiece, waiting for its miniature timekeeper to make an appearance. When the hour arrives, a small mechanical figure emerges from the clock's upper section and strikes a gong the corresponding number of times. The little performance lasts only a short while, but the anticipation in the room can make it feel like a theatrical event.The clock was acquired by Salar Jung III from the English firm Cook and Kelvey. With its intricate mechanism and moving parts, it is a reminder that clocks were once as much about craftsmanship and spectacle as they were about telling time.There is something delightfully old-fashioned about the whole experience. In an age when a glance at your phone gives you the time instantly, people still gather to watch a tiny figure do its hourly job.Travel tip: Check the clock's display schedule with museum staff when you arrive, so you can plan your visit around its performance rather than accidentally missing the moment.Plan your visitLocation: Salar Jung Road, Darulshifa, Hyderabad, Telangana 500002.Usual visiting hours: 10 am–6 pm; Friday is the weekly holiday.
